title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: "Do you know, I've been thinking about you," said Sergey Ivanovitch. "What's going on in the district is beyond anything, judging by what this doctor tells me. He's a very intelligent fellow. And as I've told you before, I tell you again: it's not right that you don't go to the meetings, that you keep out of the district business altogether. If decent men won't get involved, of course the whole thing goes wrong. We pay the money, and it all goes in salaries, and there are no schools, no district nurses, no midwives, no drugstores — nothing."
"Well, I tried, you know," Levin said slowly and unwillingly. "I can't! And there's nothing to be done about it."
"But why can't you? I'll be honest, I don't get it. Indifference, incapacity — I won't accept; surely it's not just laziness?"
"None of those things. I tried, and I see I can do nothing," Levin said.

He had barely been following what his brother was saying. Looking off toward the ploughland across the river, he could make out something black, but he could not tell whether it was a horse or the bailiff on horseback.
"Why is it you can do nothing? You made an attempt, didn't succeed — as you put it — and you give up. How can you have so little self-respect?"

"Self-respect!" said Levin, stung by his brother's words. "I don't understand. If at college they'd told me other people understood the integral calculus and I didn't, then pride would have come into it. But in this case you have to be convinced first that you have certain qualifications for this sort of work, and above all that the whole business is of great importance."

"What — do you mean to say it's not of importance?" said Sergey Ivanovitch, stung in his turn that his brother should call anything he cared about unimportant, and even more that he was so clearly paying little attention to what was being said.

"I don't think it's important; it doesn't grip me, I can't help that," Levin answered, making out that the figure was the bailiff, and that the bailiff seemed to be letting the peasants off the ploughed land. They were turning the plough over. "Could they really have finished ploughing already?" he wondered.

"Now really," said the elder brother, a crease in his handsome, clever face, "there are limits to everything. It's all very well to be original and genuine and to dislike whatever's conventional — I know all about that; but really, what you're saying either has no meaning or has a very wrong meaning. How can you think it of no importance whether the peasant, whom you love as you say —"
"I never said any such thing," Konstantin Levin thought.

"— dies without help? The ignorant peasant-women starve the children, the people stagnate in darkness and are helpless in the hands of every village clerk, while you have at your disposal a way of helping them, and don't help them because, in your mind, it's not important."
And Sergey Ivanovitch laid out the alternative: either you are so undeveloped that you can't see all you could do, or you won't sacrifice your ease, your vanity, or whatever it is, to do it.
Konstantin Levin felt there was no way out for him except to submit, or to admit to a lack of zeal for the public good. And that mortified him and hurt his feelings.
"It's both," he said firmly: "I don't see that it was possible —"
"What! Was it impossible, if the money were properly spent, to provide medical aid?"

"Impossible, as far as I can see. With the three thousand square miles of our district, with our thaws, and the storms, and the work in the fields, I don't see how medical care could be provided everywhere. And on top of that, I don't believe in medicine."
"Oh, come, that's unfair — I could quote you thousands of cases. But the schools, anyway."
"Why schools?"
"What do you mean? Is there any question that education is a good thing? If it's good for you, it's good for everyone."
Konstantin Levin felt himself morally pinned to a wall, and so he grew hot and blurted out, without thinking, the real reason for his indifference to public affairs.

"Perhaps it may all be very fine; but why should I bother myself setting up dispensaries I'll never use, and schools I'll never send my children to, that even the peasants don't want to send their children to, and that I'm not at all sure they ought to send them to?" he said.

Sergey Ivanovitch was for a moment thrown by this unexpected angle on the question; but he quickly worked out a new line of attack. He sat in silence for a little, drew out his hook, threw it back in, and turned to his brother with a smile.
"Now come — in the first place, the dispensary is needed. We ourselves sent for the district doctor for Agafea Mihalovna."
"Oh, well — I have a feeling her wrist will never be straight again."
"That remains to be seen. Next, the peasant who can read and write is a more useful, more valuable worker to you."

"No, ask anyone you like," Konstantin Levin answered firmly. "A man who can read and write is much worse as a worker. And mending the highroads is impossible; and the moment they put up a bridge, it gets stolen."

"Still, that's not the point," said Sergey Ivanovitch, frowning. He disliked being contradicted, and disliked even more arguments that kept jumping from one thing to another, throwing in new and unrelated points, so that there was no telling which one to answer. "Do you grant that education is a good thing for the people?"

"Yes, I grant it," Levin said without thinking, and at once felt he had said what he didn't mean. He saw that if he granted that, it would be proved he had been talking meaningless rubbish. How exactly it would be proved he didn't know, but he knew it would inevitably be proved to him by logic, and he braced himself for the proofs.
The argument turned out to be far simpler than he expected.
"If you grant that it is a good thing," Sergey Ivanovitch said, "then, as an honest man, you can't help caring about it and sympathizing with the movement, and therefore wanting to work for it."
"But I still don't grant that this movement is just," said Konstantin Levin, reddening a little.
"What! But you just said —"
"That is, I don't grant that it's either good or feasible."
"That you can't tell without making the trial."
"Well, suppose that's so," Levin said, though he did not at all suppose so, "suppose that's so — still, I don't see why I'm to bother myself with it."
"How so?"
"No — since we're at it, explain it to me from the philosophical point of view," Levin said.
"I don't see where philosophy comes in," Sergey Ivanovitch said, in a tone that struck Levin as not granting his brother the right to talk philosophy. And that annoyed Levin.

"I'll tell you, then," he said heatedly. "I think the mainspring of all our actions is, after all, self-interest. Now, in our local institutions, I, as a nobleman, see nothing that helps my prosperity, and the roads are not better and could not be better; my horses carry me well enough over bad ones. I have no use for doctors and dispensaries. I have no use for an arbitrator of disputes — I never appeal to him and never will. The schools are no good to me — they're actually harmful, as I've told you. For me the district institutions simply mean having to pay fourpence-halfpenny per three acres, drive into town, sleep with the bugs, and listen to all kinds of stupidity and vileness, and self-interest offers me no reason to do any of it."
"Excuse me," Sergey Ivanovitch broke in with a smile, "self-interest didn't push us to work for the emancipation of the serfs, but we worked for it."

"No!" Konstantin Levin cut in with still more heat. "The emancipation of the serfs was another matter. There, self-interest came in. We longed to throw off that yoke that crushed all decent people among us. But to be a town councilor and debate how many dustmen are needed, and how chimneys are to be built in a town I don't live in — to serve on a jury and try a peasant who's stolen a flitch of bacon, and sit for six hours straight listening to all kinds of jabber from defense and prosecution counsel, and the president cross-examining my old half-witted Alioshka, 'Do you admit, prisoner in the dock, the fact of the removal of the bacon?' 'Eh?'"
Konstantin Levin had warmed to his theme and was now imitating the president and the half-witted Alioshka: it seemed to him perfectly to the point.
But Sergey Ivanovitch shrugged.
"Well, what is it you mean to say, then?"

"I simply mean that the rights that touch me — my interest — I'll always defend as best I can; that when they raided us students and the police read our letters, I was ready to defend those rights to the utmost, to defend my rights to education and freedom. I can understand compulsory military service, which affects my children, my brothers, and myself; I'm ready to deliberate on what concerns me; but deliberating on how to spend forty thousand roubles of district council money, or on judging the half-witted Alioshka — I don't understand and I can't do it."
Konstantin Levin was speaking as if the floodgates of his speech had burst open. Sergey Ivanovitch smiled.
"But tomorrow it'll be your turn to be tried — would it have suited your tastes better to be tried in the old criminal court?"

"I'm not going to be tried. I'm not going to murder anyone, and I have no need of it. Well, I'll tell you what," he went on, flying off again onto a subject entirely beside the point, "our district self-government and all the rest of it — it's just like the birch branches we stick in the ground on Trinity Day to make it look like a copse that's grown up of itself in Europe, and I can't enthuse over these birch branches or believe in them."
Sergey Ivanovitch merely shrugged, as if to mark his surprise at how the birch branches had wandered into the argument at this point — though in fact he understood at once what his brother meant.
"Excuse me, but you really can't argue that way," he observed.
But Konstantin Levin wanted to justify himself for the failing he was aware of — his lack of zeal for the public welfare — and he kept going.

"I think," he said, "that no kind of activity is likely to last if it isn't grounded in self-interest. That's a universal principle, a philosophical principle," he said, repeating the word "philosophical" with emphasis, as if to show he had as much right to talk philosophy as anyone else.
Sergey Ivanovitch smiled. "He too has a philosophy of his own, ready to serve his natural inclinations," he thought.

"Come, you'd better leave philosophy alone," he said. "The central problem of the philosophy of every age is precisely the necessary connection between individual and social interest. But never mind that; what does matter is a correction I have to make in your comparison. The birches aren't simply stuck in; some are sown and some are planted, and one has to treat them with care. It's only those peoples that have an intuitive sense of what matters and what counts in their institutions, and know how to value them, that have a future before them — those are the only peoples one can truly call historical."
And Sergey Ivanovitch carried the discussion off into the regions of philosophical history, where Konstantin Levin could not follow him, and showed him at full length the wrongness of his view.
"As for your dislike of it, forgive me for saying so, that's simply our Russian sloth and old serf-owner's habits, and I'm sure that in you it's a passing error and will go."

Konstantin said nothing. He felt himself beaten on every side, but he also felt that what he wanted to say could not be made plain to his brother. Only he could not decide whether it was unintelligible because he wasn't capable of putting his meaning clearly, or because his brother would not or could not understand him. But he didn't pursue that thought, and without replying he fell to thinking about a quite different, personal matter.
Sergey Ivanovitch wound up the last line, untied the horse, and they drove off.

title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: The personal matter that had absorbed Levin during his conversation with his brother was this. Once, a year or two earlier, he had gone to look at the mowing, and made very angry by the bailiff, he had reached for his favorite means of regaining his temper — he had taken a scythe from a peasant and started mowing himself.

He had liked the work so much that he had tried his hand at mowing a number of times since. He had cut the whole meadow in front of his house, and ever since the early spring of this year he had been turning over the idea of mowing for entire days alongside the peasants. Since his brother's arrival he had been in two minds about it. He didn't like the thought of leaving his brother alone all day long, and he was afraid his brother would laugh at him about it. But as he drove into the meadow and remembered what mowing felt like, he very nearly made up his mind that he would go. After the irritating argument with his brother, he thought about that intention again.
"I need physical exercise — without it my temper is bound to be ruined," he thought, and he resolved to go mowing, however awkward it might be with his brother or with the peasants.

Toward evening Konstantin Levin walked over to his counting house, gave orders for the next day's work, and sent word round the village to gather the mowers for the morrow, to cut Kalinov Meadow, the largest and best of his grasslands.
"And please send my scythe over to Tit, for him to set, and have it brought back tomorrow. I may do some mowing myself," he said, trying not to sound embarrassed.
The bailiff smiled and said, "Yes, sir."
Over tea that evening, Levin said to his brother:
"I think the fine weather will hold. Tomorrow I'll start mowing."
"I'm very fond of that kind of fieldwork," said Sergey Ivanovitch.
"I love it. I sometimes mow with the peasants myself, and tomorrow I want to try mowing the whole day."
Sergey Ivanovitch lifted his head and looked at his brother with interest.
"How do you mean? Just like one of the peasants — all day long?"
"Yes, it's very pleasant," Levin said.
"It's splendid as exercise, only you'll hardly be able to stand it," Sergey Ivanovitch said, without a trace of irony.
"I've tried it. It's hard going at first, but you get into it. I think I'll be able to keep it up."
"Really? What an idea! But tell me — how do the peasants take it? I imagine they have a quiet laugh at the master's being such an odd fish?"
"No, I don't think so; but the work is so satisfying and so demanding at once, that there's no time to think about it."
"But how will you manage about dinner with them? It would be a bit awkward to send you out a bottle of Lafitte and a roast turkey."
"No, I'll just come back home at the time of their noonday rest."
Next morning Konstantin Levin got up earlier than usual, but he was held up giving directions on the farm, and by the time he reached the mowing the men were already on their second row.

From the higher ground he could see the shaded, cut stretch of meadow below, with its grayish ridges of cut grass, and the black heaps of coats the mowers had taken off at the spot where they had started cutting.

Bit by bit, as he rode toward the meadow, the peasants came into sight — some in coats, some in their shirts — mowing one behind another in a long line, swinging their scythes each in his own rhythm. He counted forty-two of them.

They were moving slowly across the uneven low-lying part of the meadow, where there had once been an old dam. Levin recognized some of his own men. There was old Yermil in a very long white smock, bent forward as he swung his scythe; there was Vaska, a young fellow who had been a coachman of Levin's, taking each row with a wide sweep. And there was Tit, Levin's master in the art of mowing — a thin little peasant. He was out ahead of them all, cutting his wide row without stooping, as if he were playing with the scythe.
Levin got down from his mare, tied her up by the roadside, and went to meet Tit, who pulled out a second scythe from a bush and handed it to him.
"It's ready, sir; like a razor, cuts of itself," Tit said, taking off his cap with a smile and giving him the scythe.

Levin took the scythe and began testing it. As they finished their rows, the mowers, hot and good-humored, came out onto the road one after another, laughing a little and greeting the master. They all stared at him, but no one said anything, until a tall old man with a wrinkled, beardless face, in a short sheepskin jacket, stepped out onto the road and spoke to him.
"Now then, master — once you take hold of the rope there's no letting go!" he said, and Levin heard smothered laughter among the mowers.
"I'll try not to let go," he said, taking his place behind Tit and waiting for the moment to start.
"Mind yourself," the old man repeated.

Tit made room, and Levin started off behind him. The grass was short close to the road, and Levin, who had not mowed for a long time and was thrown off by the eyes fixed on him, cut badly the first few moments, although he was swinging the scythe vigorously. Behind him he heard voices:
"It's not set right; the handle's too high; look at the way he has to stoop to it," said one.
"Bear more on the heel," said another.
"Never mind, he'll get on all right," the old man put in.

"He's made a start. You're swinging too wide, you'll wear yourself out. The master, sure, does his best for himself! But look at the grass missed there! For work like that the rest of us would catch it!"

The grass turned softer, and Levin, listening without answering, followed Tit, trying to do the best he could. They covered a hundred paces. Tit kept moving on, not stopping, not showing the slightest weariness, but Levin was already starting to worry that he wouldn't be able to keep it up: he was so tired.

He felt, as he swung his scythe, that he was at the very end of his strength, and he was on the point of asking Tit to stop. At that very moment Tit stopped of his own accord, bent down, picked up some grass, rubbed his scythe with it, and began whetting it. Levin straightened up, drew a deep breath, and looked around. Behind him a peasant came along, and he too was clearly tired, because he stopped at once without waiting to mow up to Levin and began whetting his scythe. Tit sharpened his own scythe and Levin's, and they went on. Next time it was the same. Tit moved on with sweep after sweep, not stopping or showing any sign of weariness. Levin followed him, trying not to fall behind, and finding it harder and harder; the moment came when he felt he had no strength left, and just then Tit stopped and whetted the scythes.

So they got through the first row. And this long row felt particularly hard to Levin; but when the end was reached and Tit, scythe on shoulder, started back at a deliberate stride over the tracks his heels had left in the cut grass, and Levin walked back in the same way along the strip he had just mown, in spite of the sweat that streamed down his face and dripped from his nose and soaked his back as though he'd been dunked in water, he felt very happy. What pleased him most was that he knew now he would be able to hold out.

His pleasure was only spoiled by the fact that his row was not well cut. "I'll swing less with my arm and more with my whole body," he thought, comparing Tit's row — which looked as if it had been laid out with a line — with his own, which lay unevenly and crookedly.

Levin had noticed that Tit had mowed the first row especially fast, probably to test his master, and the row happened to be a long one. The next rows were easier, but Levin still had to strain every nerve not to fall behind the peasants.

He thought of nothing, wanted nothing, except not to be left behind the peasants and to do his work as well as he could. He heard nothing but the swish of scythes, and he saw before him Tit's upright figure mowing on ahead, the crescent-shaped curve of the cut grass, the grass and flower heads falling slowly and rhythmically before the blade of his scythe, and ahead of him the end of the row, where the rest would come.

Suddenly, in the middle of his toil, without understanding what it was or where it came from, he felt a pleasant coolness on his hot, damp shoulders. He glanced at the sky during the next pause for whetting. A heavy, low storm cloud had blown up, and big drops of rain were falling. Some of the peasants went over to their coats and put them on; others — like Levin himself — just shrugged their shoulders, enjoying the cool of it.

Another row, and yet another row, followed — long rows and short rows, with good grass and with poor grass. Levin lost all sense of time and could not have said whether it was late or early now. A change began to come over his work, which gave him immense satisfaction. In the middle of his labor came moments when he forgot what he was doing, and it all came easy, and at those same moments his row was almost as smooth and well cut as Tit's. But as soon as he remembered what he was doing and began trying to do better, he was at once aware of all the difficulty of the task, and the row was poorly mown.

He had finished yet another row and would have gone back to the top of the meadow to begin the next, but Tit stopped, went up to the old man, and said something to him in a low voice. They both looked at the sun. "What are they talking about, and why doesn't he go back?" Levin wondered, not realizing that the peasants had been mowing for no less than four hours without a break, and that it was time for their lunch.
"Lunch, sir," the old man said.
"Is it really time? All right, then — lunch."

Levin handed his scythe back to Tit and, with the peasants — who were crossing the long stretch of mown grass, lightly sprinkled with rain, to get their bread from the heap of coats — he set off toward his house. Only then did he suddenly realize he had been wrong about the weather, and that the rain was drenching his hay.
"The hay will be spoiled," he said.
"Not a bit of it, sir; mow in the rain, and you'll rake in fine weather!" the old man said.

Levin untied his horse and rode home to his coffee. Sergey Ivanovitch was only just getting up. By the time he had drunk his coffee, Levin was riding back to the mowing before Sergey Ivanovitch had had time to dress and come down to the dining room.

title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: After lunch Levin was no longer in the same place in the line of mowers as before; he stood between the old man who had teased him earlier, and who now invited him to be his neighbor, and a young peasant who had only been married in the autumn and who was mowing this summer for the first time.

The old man, holding himself erect, moved at the front, his feet turned outward, taking long, even strides, and with a steady, precise motion that seemed to cost him no more effort than swinging one's arms in walking — as if it were a game — he laid down the tall, even row of grass. It was as if the sharp scythe itself, and not he, were swishing through the juicy grass.

Behind Levin came the lad Mishka. His pretty boyish face, with a twist of fresh grass bound around his hair, was straining hard with the effort; but whenever anyone looked at him, he smiled. He would clearly have died sooner than admit the work was hard for him.

Levin kept between them. In the worst of the day's heat the mowing did not seem so hard to him. The sweat he was drenched in cooled him, and the sun beating on his back, his head, and his arms — bare to the elbow — gave a vigor and a stubborn drive to his labor; and more and more often came those moments of unconsciousness when one could stop thinking about what one was doing. The scythe cut by itself. These were the happy moments. More delightful still were the moments when they reached the stream where the rows ended, and the old man wiped his scythe with the wet, thick grass, rinsed the blade in the fresh water of the stream, dipped out a little water in a tin dipper, and offered Levin a drink.
"What do you say to my home-brew, eh? Good, eh?" he said with a wink.

And truly Levin had never drunk any drink as good as this warm water with bits of green floating in it and a taste of rust from the tin dipper. And right after this came the delicious slow saunter back, hand on the scythe, during which he could wipe away the streaming sweat, draw deep breaths of air, and look around at the long line of mowers and at what was happening in the forest and the countryside.

The longer Levin mowed, the more often the moments of unconsciousness came over him, in which it seemed not his hands swinging the scythe, but the scythe itself doing the mowing — a body full of life and consciousness of its own — and as if by magic, without his thinking about it, the work turned out regular and well-finished on its own. These were the most blissful moments.

It was hard work only when he had to break off the motion that had become unconscious and start thinking again; when he had to mow round a hillock or a tuft of sorrel. The old man did this easily. Whenever a hillock came he changed his action, and at one moment with the heel and at another with the tip of the scythe, he clipped the hillock round both sides with short strokes. And while he did this he kept looking around and watching everything in view: at one moment he would pick a wild berry and eat it or hold it out to Levin, then he would flick away a twig with the blade of the scythe, then he would look at a quail's nest from which the bird flew up right under his scythe, or catch a snake that crossed his path and, lifting it on the scythe as if on a fork, show it to Levin and fling it aside.

For both Levin and the young peasant behind him, such changes of position were difficult. Both of them, repeating one strained movement over and over again, were in a kind of frenzy of toil and were incapable of shifting their position while watching what lay before them.

Levin had no sense of how time was passing. If asked how long he had been working, he would have said half an hour — and it was getting on for dinner time. As they were walking back over the cut grass, the old man drew Levin's attention to the little girls and boys coming from various directions, barely visible through the tall grass, and along the road toward the mowers, lugging sacks of bread that dragged at their little hands, and pitchers of sour rye beer with cloths wrapped around them.
"Look'ee, the little ants crawling!" he said, pointing to them, and he shaded his eyes with his hand to look at the sun. They mowed two more rows; the old man stopped.

"Come, master — dinner time!" he said briskly. And when they reached the stream the mowers crossed the lines of cut grass over to their pile of coats, where the children who had brought their dinners were sitting waiting. The peasants gathered into groups — those further away under a cart, those closer in under a willow bush.
Levin sat down by them; he had no wish to leave.

All shyness with the master had long since gone. The peasants got ready for dinner. Some washed, the young lads bathed in the stream, others fixed themselves a comfortable spot to rest, untied their bread sacks, and uncovered the jugs of rye beer. The old man crumbled some bread into a cup, stirred it with the handle of a spoon, poured water on it from the dipper, broke up some more bread, salted it, and then turned to the east to say his prayer.
"Come, master — try my sop," he said, kneeling down before the cup.

The sop was so good that Levin gave up the idea of going home. He had his meal with the old man, talked with him about his family matters, took the keenest interest in them, and told him about his own affairs and any details of his life that might interest the old man. He felt himself closer to him than to his own brother, and could not help smiling at the affection he felt for this man. When the old man got up again, said his prayer, and lay down under a bush, putting some grass under his head for a pillow, Levin did the same; and in spite of the clinging flies that were so persistent in the sun, and the midges that tickled his hot face and body, he fell asleep at once and only woke when the sun had moved to the other side of the bush and was reaching him. The old man had been awake a long time and was sitting up, whetting the scythes of the younger lads.

Levin looked around and hardly recognized the place, everything was so changed. The huge stretch of meadow had been mown and was sparkling with a peculiar fresh brilliance, its rows of already sweet-smelling grass laid out in the slanting evening sun. The bushes around the river had been cut down, the river itself, hidden before, was now gleaming like steel in its bends, and the moving, rising line of peasants, and the sharp wall of grass of the unmown part of the meadow, and the hawks hovering over the stripped meadow — all of it was perfectly new. Raising himself, Levin began calculating how much had been cut and how much more could still be done that day.

The work done was uncommonly large for forty-two men. They had cut the whole of the big meadow, which back in the days of serf labor had taken thirty scythes two days to mow. Only the corners were left, where the rows were short. But Levin felt a longing to get as much mown that day as possible, and was vexed that the sun was sinking so quickly. He felt no weariness at all; he only wanted to get the work done more and more quickly, and as much of it as possible.
"Could you cut Mashkin Upland too, do you think?" he said to the old man.
"As God wills — the sun's not high yet. A little vodka for the lads?"
At the afternoon rest, when they were sitting down again and those who smoked had lit their pipes, the old man told the men that "Mashkin Upland's to be cut — there'll be some vodka."
"Why not cut it? Come on, Tit! We'll look sharp! We can eat at night. Come on!" voices cried, and finishing off their bread, the mowers went back to work.
"Come, lads, keep it up!" Tit said, and ran on ahead at almost a trot.
"Get along, get along!" the old man said, hurrying after him and easily overtaking him. "I'll mow you down, look out!"

And young and old mowed away as if racing one another. But for all their speed, they did not spoil the grass, and the rows were laid down just as neatly and exactly as before. The little patch left uncut in the corner was mown in five minutes. The last of the mowers were just finishing their rows while the first ones flung their coats over their shoulders and crossed the road toward Mashkin Upland.

The sun was already sinking into the trees when, with their jingling dippers, they entered the wooded ravine of Mashkin Upland. The grass was waist-high in the middle of the hollow, soft, tender, and feathery, dotted here and there among the trees with wild heart's-ease.

After a brief consultation — whether to take the rows lengthwise or diagonally — Prohor Yermilin, another famous mower, a huge, black-haired peasant, went on ahead. He climbed to the top, turned back, and started mowing, and all the others fell in behind him, going downhill through the hollow and uphill right up to the edge of the forest. The sun sank behind the trees. The dew was falling now; the mowers were in the sun only on the hillside, but below, where a mist was rising, and on the opposite slope, they mowed into fresh, dewy shadow. The work went on quickly. The grass cut with a juicy sound and was at once laid in high, fragrant rows. The mowers from every side, drawn close together in the short row, kept urging each other on with jingling dippers and clanging scythes and the hiss of whetstones sharpening them, and with good-humored shouts.

Levin still kept between the young peasant and the old man. The old man, who had put on his short sheepskin jacket, was just as good-humored, just as full of jokes, just as free in his movements as before. Among the trees they kept cutting with their scythes the so-called "birch mushrooms," swollen fat in the lush grass. But every time the old man came across a mushroom he bent down, picked it up, and tucked it into his shirt. "Another present for my old woman," he said as he did so.

Easy as it was to mow the wet, soft grass, it was hard work going up and down the steep sides of the ravine. But it didn't trouble the old man. Swinging his scythe just as ever, taking firm little steps with his feet in their big plaited shoes, he climbed slowly up the steep stretch, and although his breeches hung out below his smock and his whole frame shook with effort, he didn't miss a single blade of grass or a single mushroom along the way, and went on cracking jokes with the peasants and with Levin. Levin walked behind him and kept thinking he was bound to fall, as he climbed with a scythe up a steep face where it would have been hard work to climb without anything in your hands. But up he went, and did what he had to do. He felt as if some external force were carrying him along.

title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: Mashkin Upland was finished, the last row mown, and the peasants pulled on their coats and trudged home in good spirits. Levin climbed onto his horse, took regretful leave of them, and rode back toward the house. From the hillside he turned to look. The mist had come up from the valley and swallowed them — all he could catch were rough, cheerful voices, bursts of laughter, and the clank of scythes.

Sergey Ivanovitch had finished dinner long ago and was sitting in his own room with a glass of iced lemon water, paging through the reviews and papers that had just arrived in the post, when Levin burst in chattering happily — hair wet and matted against his forehead, back and chest streaked with grime and sweat.
"We cut the whole meadow! Oh, it's wonderful, it's marvelous! And how have you been getting on?" Levin said, the unpleasant conversation of the day before entirely gone from his mind.

"Good heavens, look at the state of you!" said Sergey Ivanovitch, glancing round for a moment with some displeasure. "And the door — shut the door, do!" he cried. "You must have let in a dozen of them at least."
Sergey Ivanovitch could not bear flies. In his own room he kept the window shut except at night, and was strict about keeping the door closed.
"Not one, I swear. And if I have, I'll catch them for you. You can't imagine the pleasure of it! How did you spend the day?"
"Very pleasantly. But have you really been mowing the whole day? I expect you're starving. Kouzma has everything waiting for you."
"No, I'm not even hungry. I ate something out there. But I'll go and wash up."

"Yes, off you go, off you go, and I'll join you in a moment," said Sergey Ivanovitch, shaking his head as he watched his brother. "Off with you, hurry up," he added, smiling, and he gathered up his books and got ready to go as well. He had suddenly turned cheerful himself and felt no inclination to leave his brother's side. "But what did you do when it was raining?"
"Rain? There was barely a drop. I'll be there in a minute. So you had a good day too? Excellent." And Levin went off to change.

Five minutes later the brothers met in the dining room. Although Levin had thought he wasn't hungry and was only sitting down so as not to offend Kouzma, the food struck him as extraordinarily good the moment he began. Sergey Ivanovitch watched him with a smile.
"Oh, by the way — there's a letter for you," he said. "Kouzma, bring it down, please. And mind you shut the doors."

The letter was from Oblonsky. Levin read it out. Oblonsky was writing from Petersburg: "I've had a letter from Dolly. She's at Ergushovo, and everything seems to be falling apart there. Do ride over and see her, please — give her some advice, you know how these things go. She'll be delighted to see you. She's all on her own, poor thing. My mother-in-law and the rest of them are still abroad."
"That's perfect! I'll certainly ride over," said Levin. "Or we'll go together. She's a splendid woman, isn't she?"
"They're not far from here, then?"
"Twenty-five miles. Maybe thirty. But the road is excellent. Excellent — we'll drive over."
"I'd be delighted," said Sergey Ivanovitch, still smiling. The sight of his younger brother had put him at once into a good mood.
"You do have an appetite!" he said, looking at the sunburnt, dark-red face and neck bent over the plate.
"Magnificent! You can't imagine how effective a remedy it is against every kind of nonsense. I want to give medicine a new word for it: _Arbeitskur_."
"Well, you don't need it, I should think."
"No, but for all those nervous patients."

"Yes, it should be tried. I had meant to come out to the mowing to see you, but the heat was so unbearable I got no further than the forest. I sat there a while, then walked on through the woods to the village. I ran into your old nurse and sounded her out on what the peasants make of you. As far as I can gather, they don't approve. She said, 'It's not a gentleman's work.' On the whole I suspect that in the people's minds there are very clear and definite notions about what counts as 'gentlemanly' behavior. And they don't sanction it when the gentry step outside the lines they've drawn."

"Maybe so — but the fact is it's a pleasure I've never known in my life. And there's no harm in it, is there?" Levin answered. "I can't help it if they don't like it. Still, I think it's all right. Eh?"
"All in all," Sergey Ivanovitch went on, "you're satisfied with your day?"
"Quite satisfied. We cut the whole meadow. And the marvelous old man I made friends with out there! You can't imagine how delightful he was."

"Well, so you're content with your day, and so am I. First, I solved two chess problems — one of them very pretty, a pawn opening. I'll show it to you. And then I thought over our conversation yesterday."

"Eh? Our conversation yesterday?" said Levin, blissfully half-closing his eyes and breathing deeply now that he had finished his dinner, completely unable to recall what their conversation yesterday had been about.

"I think you're partly right. Our disagreement comes down to this: you make self-interest the mainspring, while I assume that an interest in the common good is bound to exist in any man past a certain stage of development. Perhaps you're right too, that action grounded in material interest would be more effective. You're altogether, as the French say, too _primesautière_ a nature — you have to have intense, energetic action, or none at all."

Levin listened to his brother without taking in a single word, and without any desire to take it in. His only fear was that his brother might ask him something that would expose him for not having listened.
"That's how I see it, my dear boy," said Sergey Ivanovitch, touching him on the shoulder.

"Yes, of course. But you know — I won't insist on my view," Levin answered with a guilty, childlike smile. "Whatever was it I was arguing about?" he wondered. "Of course, I'm right and he's right and it's all fine. Only I have to go round to the counting house and see to things." He got up, stretching and smiling. Sergey Ivanovitch smiled too.

"If you're going out, let's go together," he said, reluctant to part from his brother, who seemed to be exhaling freshness and energy. "Come, we'll walk to the counting house if you need to go there."
"Oh, heavens!" Levin shouted — so loudly that Sergey Ivanovitch was startled.
"What — what is it?"
"How's Agafea Mihalovna's hand?" said Levin, slapping his forehead. "I'd completely forgotten about her."
"Much better."
"Even so, I'll dash down to her. Before you've had time to put your hat on, I'll be back."
And he ran downstairs, his heels clattering like a wooden rattle.

title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch had gone to Petersburg to perform the most natural and indispensable of official duties — the one familiar to everyone in government service though incomprehensible to outsiders: that ritual without which a man could hardly remain in the service at all, of reminding the ministry that he still existed. Having taken all the available cash from home in order to perform the rite properly, he was now spending his days agreeably at the races and the summer villas. Meanwhile Dolly and the children had moved to the country to cut expenses as far as they could. She had gone to Ergushovo, the estate that had been her dowry — the same one where the forest had been sold in the spring. It was nearly forty miles from Levin's Pokrovskoe. The big old house at Ergushovo had been pulled down long ago; the old prince had had the lodge refurbished and added onto. Twenty years earlier, when Dolly was a child, the lodge had been roomy and comfortable, though, like all lodges, it stood sideways to the entrance avenue and faced south. By now, however, the place was old and dilapidated. When Stepan Arkadyevitch had gone down in the spring to sell the forest, Dolly had begged him to look the house over and order whatever repairs were needed. Like all unfaithful husbands, Stepan Arkadyevitch was very attentive to his wife's comfort, and he had looked the house over himself and given instructions about whatever he deemed necessary. What he deemed necessary was to cover the furniture in cretonne, hang curtains, weed the garden, build a little bridge over the pond, and plant flowers. But he forgot a great many other essentials, the absence of which would later cause Darya Alexandrovna a great deal of grief.

However hard Stepan Arkadyevitch tried to play the attentive father and husband, he could never quite hold in his head the fact that he had a wife and children. He had bachelor tastes, and he organized his life around them. On his return to Moscow he announced proudly to his wife that everything was ready, that the house would be a little paradise, and that he strongly advised her to go. Having his wife away in the country suited Stepan Arkadyevitch from every angle: it was good for the children, it cut expenses, and it gave him more freedom. Darya Alexandrovna, for her part, regarded a summer in the country as essential for the children — especially for the little girl, who hadn't fully recovered her strength after the scarlatina — and as a way of escaping the petty humiliations, the small bills owed to the wood merchant, the fishmonger, and the shoemaker, that left her miserable. There was a further reason she was glad to go: she had been dreaming of persuading her sister Kitty to come and stay. Kitty was due back from abroad in midsummer, and bathing had been prescribed for her. Kitty wrote that nothing sounded as inviting as a summer with Dolly at Ergushovo, a place full of childhood memories for both of them.

The first days in the country were hard on Dolly. She had spent summers there as a child, and her memory of it was of a refuge from all the annoyances of town — a place where life, if not luxurious (and Dolly could easily resign herself to that), was cheap and easy, where everything was plentiful and inexpensive, everything could be had, and the children were happy. But arriving now as the head of the household, she found that the reality was nothing like the picture in her memory.

The day after they arrived, there was a heavy downpour, and overnight the water came through into the corridor and the nursery, so that the beds had to be dragged into the drawing room. There was no kitchen maid to be found. Of the nine cows, according to the cowherd-woman, some were about to calve, some had just calved, others were old, and others had hard udders — there wasn't enough butter or milk for the children. There were no eggs. They couldn't get any fowls; all they had to roast or boil were old, purplish, stringy cocks. There were no women to be had to scrub the floors — every one of them was off hoeing potatoes. Driving was out of the question because one of the horses was restive and bolted in the shafts. There was no place to bathe; the entire riverbank was trampled by cattle and exposed to the road. Even walks were impossible — the cattle wandered into the garden through a gap in the hedge, and one of them was a terrible bull who bellowed and was sure, sooner or later, to gore someone. There were no proper wardrobes for their clothes: the ones that existed either wouldn't close at all or sprang open whenever anyone walked past. There were no pots and pans, no copper boiler in the wash-house, not even an ironing board in the maids' room.

Finding, instead of peace and rest, this string of (from her point of view) appalling calamities, Darya Alexandrovna was at first in despair. She worked herself to the limit, felt how hopeless the situation was, and kept choking back tears every other minute. The bailiff, a retired quartermaster whom Stepan Arkadyevitch had taken a liking to and appointed on the strength of his handsome, deferential, hall-porter sort of bearing, showed no sympathy at all for Darya Alexandrovna's troubles. He would say respectfully, "There's nothing to be done — the peasants are a hopeless lot," and do nothing to help.

It looked hopeless. But in the Oblonsky household, as in every household, there was one inconspicuous yet invaluable and useful person — Marya Philimonovna. She soothed her mistress, assured her that everything would _come round_ (that was her expression, which Matvey had borrowed from her), and without fuss or hurry set to work herself. Almost at once she made friends with the bailiff's wife, and on the very first day she sat under the acacias drinking tea with her and the bailiff, going over the whole situation. Before long Marya Philimonovna had established her club, so to speak, under the acacias, and it was in this club, made up of the bailiff's wife, the village elder, and the counting-house clerk, that one difficulty after another was gradually smoothed away — and within a week everything really had come round. The roof was mended, a kitchen maid was found (a crony of the village elder's), hens were bought, the cows began to give milk, the gap in the garden hedge was blocked up with stakes, the carpenter made a mangle, hooks were fitted into the cupboards so that they stopped flying open, and an ironing board covered in army cloth was set up between a chair-arm and the chest of drawers — and the smell of flatirons filled the maids' room.

"There — and you were quite in despair," said Marya Philimonovna, pointing to the ironing board. They even rigged up a bathing-shed out of straw hurdles. Lily began to bathe, and Darya Alexandrovna began to glimpse, at least in part, what she had been hoping for: if not peaceful, at least comfortable country life. Peaceful with six children, Darya Alexandrovna couldn't possibly be. One would fall ill, another might easily go the same way, a third would be short of something essential, a fourth would start showing signs of a bad disposition, and so on. The brief patches of calm were rare indeed. But for Darya Alexandrovna these worries and anxieties were the only happiness available. Without them she would have been left alone to brood over the husband who didn't love her. And, hard as it was for a mother to live in dread of illness, to live through the illnesses themselves, to spot signs of bad tendencies in her children, the children themselves were already paying her back in small joys for her suffering. Those joys were so small that they passed unnoticed, like grains of gold in sand, and in bad moments she saw nothing but the pain — nothing but sand. But there were good moments too, when she saw nothing but the joy, nothing but the gold.

Now, in the solitude of the country, she was becoming aware of these joys more and more often. Watching her children, she would do everything she could to convince herself that she was deluded, that as a mother she was naturally biased. All the same, she couldn't help admitting to herself that she had charming children, all six of them in different ways — a set of children of a kind one didn't often come across — and that she was happy in them and proud of them.

title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Toward the end of May, when things had been more or less satisfactorily arranged, she received her husband's reply to her complaints about the disorganized state of things in the country. He wrote begging her forgiveness for not having thought of everything in advance and promised to come down at the first opportunity. The opportunity never presented itself, and Darya Alexandrovna remained alone in the country until the beginning of June.

On the Sunday during St. Peter's week, Darya Alexandrovna drove to mass so that all her children could take the sacrament. In her intimate, philosophical conversations with her sister, her mother, and her friends, Darya Alexandrovna often startled them with how freely she viewed religion. She had her own strange creed about the transmigration of souls, which she firmly believed, troubling herself little over the Church's doctrines. But within her own family she was strict about everything the Church required — and not merely to set an example, but with her whole heart behind it. The fact that the children had not been to the sacrament for nearly a year was a source of real worry to her, and with Marya Philimonovna's full approval and sympathy, she decided that it should happen now in the summer.

For several days beforehand, Darya Alexandrovna was busy deliberating how to dress all the children. Dresses were made up or altered and washed, seams and flounces let out, buttons sewn on, ribbons set ready. One dress — Tanya's, which the English governess had taken on — cost Darya Alexandrovna a great deal of patience. The English governess had put the seams in the wrong places, taken the sleeves in too far, and altogether ruined it. It was so tight across Tanya's shoulders that it was painful to look at her. But Marya Philimonovna had the happy idea of inserting gussets and adding a little shoulder-cape. The dress was put right, but there was nearly a quarrel with the English governess. By morning, however, all was happily arranged, and toward ten o'clock — the time at which they had asked the priest to wait for them for mass — the children, in their new dresses, faces beaming, stood on the step in front of the carriage waiting for their mother.

Instead of the restive Raven, they had — thanks to Marya Philimonovna's intervention — harnessed the bailiff's horse, Brownie. Darya Alexandrovna, who had been delayed by worry over her own outfit, came out and got in, dressed in a white muslin gown.

Darya Alexandrovna had done her hair and dressed with care and a touch of excitement. Once upon a time she had dressed for herself, to look pretty and be admired. Later, as she got older, dressing had become more and more distasteful to her. She could see she was losing her looks. But now she felt pleasure and interest in dress again. Now she was not dressing for her own sake, not for her own beauty, but simply so that, as the mother of these exquisite creatures, she wouldn't spoil the overall effect. Looking herself over one last time in the mirror, she was satisfied. She looked nice. Not nice in the way she would have liked to look in the old days at a ball, but nice for what she was setting out to do now.

In the church there was no one but peasants, servants, and their womenfolk. But Darya Alexandrovna either saw, or imagined she saw, the sensation her children and she made. The children weren't only beautiful to look at in their smart little dresses — they behaved charmingly too. Aliosha, it's true, didn't stand quite properly: he kept turning around to try and see his little jacket from behind. But even so he was wonderfully sweet. Tanya behaved like a grown-up and looked after the little ones. And the smallest, Lily, was enchanting in her naive astonishment at everything, and it was hard not to smile when, after taking the sacrament, she said in English, "Please, some more."
On the way home the children sensed that something solemn had taken place and were very quiet.

Everything went happily at home too — but at lunch Grisha started whistling and, worse, was rude to the English governess, and was forbidden any tart. Darya Alexandrovna wouldn't have let things go that far on such a day if she'd been there, but she had to back the English governess's authority and upheld the ruling that Grisha get no tart. This rather spoiled the general good mood. Grisha cried, insisting that Nikolinka had whistled too and hadn't been punished, and that he wasn't crying for the tart — he didn't care about the tart — but at being treated unfairly. It was really too tragic, and Darya Alexandrovna made up her mind to persuade the English governess to forgive Grisha. She went to speak to her — but on the way, as she passed the drawing room, she came on a scene that filled her heart with such pleasure that tears sprang to her eyes, and she forgave the offender herself.

The culprit was sitting at the window in the corner of the drawing room. Beside him stood Tanya with a plate. On the pretext of wanting to give her dolls some dinner, she had asked the governess's permission to take her share of the tart to the nursery, and had taken it instead to her brother. While still weeping over the injustice of his punishment, he was eating the tart, repeating through his sobs, "Eat some yourself — let's eat it together... together."
Tanya had at first been moved by pity for Grisha, then by a sense of her own noble action, and tears were standing in her eyes too — but she didn't refuse, and ate her share.

On catching sight of their mother they were dismayed, but, studying her face, they saw they were not in trouble. They burst out laughing and, with their mouths full of tart, began wiping their smiling lips on the backs of their hands and smearing their radiant faces all over with tears and jam.
"Goodness! Your new white frock! Tanya! Grisha!" their mother said, trying to save the frock — but with tears in her eyes and a blissful, rapturous smile on her face.

The new frocks were taken off, and orders were given for the little girls to be put into their blouses and the boys into their old jackets, and for the wagonette to be harnessed (with Brownie, to the bailiff's annoyance, in the shafts again) to take them out for mushroom-picking and a swim. A roar of delighted shrieks went up in the nursery and didn't subside until they had set off for the bathing place.

They gathered a whole basketful of mushrooms — even Lily found a birch mushroom. Up to now Miss Hoole had always been the one to spot them and point them out, but this time Lily found a big one entirely by herself, and a general scream of delight went up: "Lily's found a mushroom!"

Then they reached the river, parked the horses under the birch trees, and went down to the bathing place. The coachman, Terenty, tethered the horses, who kept whisking the flies away, to a tree, and lay down in the shade of a birch, trampling the grass flat, and smoked his shag while the unending shrieks of delight from the children drifted across to him from the bathing place.

Hard as it was to keep track of every child and rein in their wildness, hard as it was to keep all the stockings, little breeches, and shoes from getting mixed up between the various pairs of legs, and to undo and do up all the tapes and buttons again, Darya Alexandrovna — who had always loved bathing herself and believed it was very good for the children — enjoyed nothing as much as bathing with the whole flock. To work her way around all those plump little legs, pulling on their stockings, to gather those little naked bodies into her arms and dip them into the water and listen to their cries of delight and alarm, to see the breathless faces with wide-open, frightened, happy eyes — all her splashing cherubs — was a tremendous pleasure to her.

When half the children were dressed, some peasant women in holiday clothes, out picking herbs, came up to the bathing shed and stopped shyly. Marya Philimonovna called one of them over and handed her a sheet and a shirt that had dropped into the water to be dried, and Darya Alexandrovna started to talk to them. At first they laughed behind their hands and didn't follow her questions, but they soon grew bolder and began to talk, and they won Darya Alexandrovna's heart on the spot with the genuine admiration they showed for the children.
"My, what a beauty! white as sugar," said one, admiring Tanitchka, and shaking her head; "but thin..."
"Yes, she's been ill."
"And so they've been bathing you too," said another to the baby.
"No — he's only three months old," answered Darya Alexandrovna proudly.
"You don't say so!"
"And do you have any children?"
"I've had four — two living, a boy and a girl. I weaned her last carnival."
"How old is she?"
"Two years old."
"Why did you nurse her so long?"
"It's our custom — three fasts..."
And the conversation became fascinating to Darya Alexandrovna. What kind of time had she had? What was wrong with the boy? Where was her husband? Did it happen often?

Darya Alexandrovna had no wish to leave the peasant women — their talk was so interesting to her, their concerns so entirely shared. What pleased her most of all was that she could see clearly that what they admired more than anything was her having so many children, and such fine ones. The peasant women even made Darya Alexandrovna laugh, and offended the English governess, because she was the cause of laughter she couldn't understand. One of the younger women kept staring at the Englishwoman, who was dressing after all the rest, and when she put on her third petticoat she couldn't hold back the comment, "My, she keeps on putting them on and putting them on, and she'll never have done!" — and they all went off into peals of laughter.

title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: On the drive home, with all her children gathered around her — their heads still damp from the bath, a kerchief tied over her own — Darya Alexandrovna was nearing the house when the coachman said, "There's a gentleman coming up: the master of Pokrovskoe, I do believe."

Darya Alexandrovna leaned forward and was delighted to recognize, in the gray hat and gray coat walking toward them, the familiar figure of Levin. She was always glad to see him, but this particular moment was especially welcome — there was no one better placed than Levin to appreciate her in her full glory.
Catching sight of her, he found himself looking straight at one of the scenes from his daydream of family life.
"You're a hen with her chicks, Darya Alexandrovna."
"Oh, I'm so glad to see you!" she said, holding out her hand.
"Glad to see me — but you didn't let me know. My brother is staying with me. I got a note from Stiva saying you were here."
"From Stiva?" Darya Alexandrovna asked, surprised.

"Yes. He writes that you're down here and thinks you might let me be of some use to you," Levin said, and saying it he was suddenly embarrassed. He broke off mid-sentence and walked on in silence beside the wagonette, snapping off lime-tree buds and chewing them. He was embarrassed because he sensed that Darya Alexandrovna would dislike being offered, by an outsider, the kind of help that ought by rights to come from her own husband. And Darya Alexandrovna certainly did not care for this habit of Stepan Arkadyevitch's of palming off his domestic duties on others. She was at once aware that Levin was aware of it. It was precisely for this kind of fine perception, this delicacy, that she liked him.

"I understand, of course," Levin went on, "that all it really means is that you wouldn't mind seeing me, and I'm extremely glad you wouldn't. Still, I can imagine that, used as you are to running a household in town, you must feel a bit lost out here in the wilds — and if anything's needed, I'm entirely at your disposal."

"Oh, no!" said Dolly. "At first things were rather difficult, but now we've got everything sorted out beautifully — thanks to my old nurse," she said, gesturing at Marya Philimonovna, who, sensing she was being spoken of, beamed at Levin in warm welcome. She knew him, knew he would make a fine match for her young lady, and was very eager to see the matter settled.
"Won't you climb in, sir? We can make room on this side," she said to him.

"No, I'll walk. Children — who wants to race the horses with me?" The children barely knew Levin and couldn't remember when they had last seen him, but they felt none of that strange shyness and hostility children so often feel toward false-fronted grown-ups — the feeling for which they are so often, and so miserably, punished. Hypocrisy of any kind may take in the cleverest and most penetrating adult, but the dimmest child spots it and recoils, however cunningly it has been dressed up. Whatever faults Levin had, hypocrisy wasn't among them, and the children responded to him with the same friendliness they read in their mother's face. At his invitation the two older ones leapt straight out and ran along with him as easily as they would have with their nurse or Miss Hoole or their mother. Lily, too, began begging to be let down to him, and her mother handed her over; he settled her on his shoulder and ran on.
"Don't worry, don't worry, Darya Alexandrovna!" he called, smiling cheerfully back at the mother. "There's no chance I'll hurt her or drop her."
And, watching his strong, agile, exaggeratedly careful and quite needlessly anxious movements, the mother relaxed and smiled brightly back at him in approval.

Out here in the country, with the children, and with Darya Alexandrovna — whose company suited him — Levin slipped into a mood that came over him often: a kind of boyish high spirits that she found particularly endearing. As he ran with the children he showed them gymnastic tricks, set Miss Hoole laughing with his odd English accent, and told Darya Alexandrovna about his work on the estate.
After dinner, sitting alone with him on the balcony, Darya Alexandrovna brought up Kitty.
"You know, Kitty's coming down — she's going to spend the summer with me."

"Really," he said, going red, and immediately, to change the subject: "Then I'll send you over two cows, shall I? If you insist on a bill, you'll pay me five roubles a month — but it's really too bad of you."
"No, thank you. We're managing perfectly well now."
"Oh, well, then, I'll have a look at your cows, and, if you'll allow me, I'll give some instructions about their feed. The feed is everything."

And Levin, to keep the conversation on safer ground, laid out for Darya Alexandrovna his theory of cow-keeping, founded on the principle that a cow is simply a machine for converting feed into milk, and so on.

He kept talking about all this, while what he passionately wanted was to hear more about Kitty — and at the same time he was afraid of hearing it. He dreaded the breaking of the inner peace he had won with such effort.
"Yes, but somebody has to keep track of all that, and who's to do it?" Darya Alexandrovna answered, with no real interest.

By now, thanks to Marya Philimonovna, she had got her household arrangements running so satisfactorily that she had no wish to disturb them; and besides, she had no faith in Levin's grasp of farming. General principles about the cow as a milk-producing machine struck her as suspect. It seemed to her that principles of that kind could only get in the way of managing a farm. To her the whole thing was much simpler: as Marya Philimonovna had explained, all you had to do was feed and water Brindle and Whitebreast better and stop the cook from carrying every bit of kitchen slop off to the laundry maid's cow. That much was clear. General propositions about meal feed and grass feed were doubtful and murky. And above all, she wanted to talk about Kitty.

title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: "Kitty writes that there's nothing she longs for so much as quiet and solitude," Dolly said, after the silence that had settled between them.
"And how is she — better?" Levin asked, his agitation showing.
"Thank God, she's quite well again. I never believed her lungs were affected."
"Oh, I'm so glad!" said Levin, and Dolly thought she caught something touching, something helpless, in his face as he said it and looked silently at her.
"Let me ask you something, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," said Darya Alexandrovna, with her kindly, faintly mocking smile. "Why are you angry with Kitty?"
"I? I'm not angry with her," Levin said.
"Yes, you are. Why did you not come to see us, or to see them, when you were in Moscow?"

"Darya Alexandrovna," he said, blushing to the roots of his hair, "I'm really surprised that with your kind heart you can't feel this. How can you have no pity for me, if nothing else, when you know...."
"What is it I know?"
"You know I made an offer and that I was refused," said Levin, and all the tenderness he had been feeling for Kitty a moment before was swept aside by a wave of anger at the injury he had suffered.
"What makes you suppose I know?"
"Because everyone knows it...."
"That's exactly where you're mistaken. I didn't know, though I'd guessed."
"Well, now you know."

"All I knew was that something had happened that had made her terribly unhappy, and that she'd begged me never to speak of it. If she wouldn't tell me, she certainly wouldn't have told anyone else. But what did happen between you? Tell me."
"I've told you."
"When was it?"
"The last time I was at their house."
"Do you know," said Darya Alexandrovna, "I am terribly, terribly sorry for her. You are only suffering from pride...."
"Perhaps," said Levin, "but...."
She interrupted him.
"But she, poor girl... I'm terribly, terribly sorry for her. Now I can see all of it."
"Well, Darya Alexandrovna, you'll have to excuse me," he said, getting up. "Goodbye, Darya Alexandrovna, till next time."
"No, wait a moment," she said, catching him by the sleeve. "Wait a minute, sit down."
"Please, please, let's not talk about this," he said, sitting down again, and at the same time feeling a hope he had believed buried lift and stir inside him.
"If I didn't like you," she said, and tears welled up in her eyes, "if I didn't know you the way I do...."
The feeling that had seemed dead kept rising in him, taking hold of Levin's heart.

"Yes, now I understand the whole thing," said Darya Alexandrovna. "You can't grasp it; for you men, who are free and who get to choose, it's always perfectly clear who you love. But a girl is left in suspense, with all the modesty of a woman, of a maiden — a girl who sees you men only from a distance, who takes everything on trust — she may, and very often does, find herself feeling something she has no idea how to put into words."
"Yes, if the heart doesn't speak...."

"No, the heart does speak. But think about it: you men form your view of a girl, you call at the house, you make friends, you weigh her up, you wait to see whether you've found what you want — and then, once you're certain you love her, you propose...."
"Well, it's not quite like that."

"Either way, you propose when your love is ripe, or when the balance has tipped clearly between the two you're choosing between. But a girl isn't asked. She's expected to do the choosing — and yet she can't really choose, she can only answer 'yes' or 'no.'"
"Yes, choose between me and Vronsky," Levin thought, and the dead thing that had stirred to life inside him died again, leaving only a weight on his heart and a dull ache.
"Darya Alexandrovna," he said, "that's how one chooses a new dress, or some purchase — not love. The choice has been made, and so much the better.... There can be no doing it over."

"Oh, pride, pride!" said Darya Alexandrovna, as if she despised him for the cheapness of this feeling next to the other one, which only women know. "At the moment when you proposed to Kitty, she was precisely in a position where she could not give you an answer. She was torn. Torn between you and Vronsky. She was seeing him every day, and you she hadn't seen for a long while. If she'd been older... I, for instance, in her place, couldn't have hesitated. I disliked him from the start, and it has all turned out as I expected."
Levin remembered Kitty's words. She had said: "_No, that cannot be_...."

"Darya Alexandrovna," he said dryly, "I appreciate your trust in me; I think you're making a mistake. But whether I'm right or wrong, that pride you so despise makes any thought of Katerina Alexandrovna impossible for me — you understand, completely out of the question."

"I'll only say one more thing: remember that I'm speaking of my sister, whom I love as I love my own children. I'm not saying she cared for you — I only mean that her refusal at that moment proves nothing."

"I don't know!" said Levin, jumping to his feet. "If you knew how much you're hurting me. It's just as if a child of yours had died and someone were to say to you: he would have grown up like this and like that, he might have lived, and how happy you would have been with him. But he's dead, dead, dead!..."

"How absurd you are!" said Darya Alexandrovna, watching Levin's outburst with a sad tenderness. "Yes, I see it more and more clearly," she went on, almost to herself. "So you won't come to see us, then, when Kitty's here?"
"No, I won't. Of course I won't go out of my way to avoid Katerina Alexandrovna, but as far as I can, I'll spare her the annoyance of having to see me."

"You really are absurd," Darya Alexandrovna repeated, looking tenderly into his face. "All right, then — we'll act as though we never spoke of it. Tanya, what is it?" she said in French to the little girl who had come in.
"Where's my spade, mamma?"
"I'm speaking French, and you must too."

The little girl tried to repeat the question in French, but couldn't remember the French for spade; her mother supplied it, then told her in French where to look for it. And this jarred unpleasantly on Levin.

Everything in Darya Alexandrovna's house and in her children seemed to him now nothing like as charming as it had a little while ago. "And what does she speak French with the children for?" he thought. "How unnatural and false it is — and the children feel it. Learning French and unlearning truthfulness," he thought to himself, unaware that Darya Alexandrovna had already turned all that over in her own mind twenty times — and had concluded that even at the cost of some sincerity, the children had to be taught French in just this way.
"But why are you going? Stay a little longer."
Levin stayed for tea, but his good humor had drained away, and he felt uncomfortable.

After tea he went out into the hall to order his horses brought round, and when he came back he found Darya Alexandrovna deeply upset, her face troubled and her eyes full of tears. While Levin had been outside, something had happened that demolished all the happiness she had felt that day and all the pride she had been taking in her children. Grisha and Tanya had been fighting over a ball. Hearing a scream from the nursery, Darya Alexandrovna had run in to a terrible sight. Tanya was pulling Grisha's hair, while he, his face hideous with rage, was hitting her with his fists wherever he could land a blow. Something snapped inside Darya Alexandrovna at the sight. It was as if darkness had come down over her life: these children of hers, of whom she had been so proud, were not just ordinary children but actually bad ones — badly brought up, with coarse, brutal instincts. Wicked children.
She couldn't think or speak of anything else, and she couldn't share her misery with Levin.

Levin could see she was unhappy and tried to comfort her, saying it didn't prove anything, that all children fight; but even as he said it, he was thinking: "No, I won't go in for any of that play-acting and talk French with my children — but my children won't be like that. All you have to do is not spoil children, not warp their nature, and they'll be lovely. No, my children won't be like that."
He said goodbye and drove off, and she made no attempt to keep him.

title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: In the middle of July the village elder from Levin's sister's estate — about fifteen miles from Pokrovskoe — came to Levin to report on how things were going there, and in particular on the hay. The chief source of income on that estate was the riverside meadows. In earlier years the peasants had bought the hay at twenty roubles for three acres. When Levin took over running the estate he looked the grasslands over and decided they were worth more, so he set the price at twenty-five roubles for three acres. The peasants refused to pay it and, as Levin suspected, kept other buyers away. Then he drove over himself and arranged to have the grass cut, partly with hired labor and partly in return for a share of the crop. His own peasants threw every obstacle they could in the way of this new arrangement, but it went through, and the first year the meadows brought in nearly double the profit. The year before — the third year — the peasants had kept up the same resistance, and the hay had been cut on the same system. This year they were doing all the mowing for a third of the crop, and the village elder had come now to report that the hay was cut; that, fearing rain, they had called the counting-house clerk over, divided the crop in his presence, and raked together eleven stacks as the owner's share. From the vague answers to his questions about how much hay had come off the main meadow, from the haste of the elder in carrying out the division without authorization, from the man's whole tone, Levin sensed that something was off about the way the hay had been divided, and he resolved to drive over and look into it himself.

Arriving at the village around dinner-time, and leaving his horse at the cottage of an old friend — the husband of his brother's wet-nurse — Levin went to find the old man in his bee-house, hoping to get the truth about the hay out of him. Parmenitch, a talkative, fine-looking old man, gave Levin a warm welcome, showed him everything he had on hand, told him all about his bees and that season's swarms — but gave vague, reluctant answers to Levin's questions about the mowing. This confirmed Levin's suspicions further. He went down to the hay fields and looked over the stacks. There was no way these stacks contained fifty wagon-loads each, and to prove the point Levin ordered the wagons that had hauled the hay to be brought up right away, told the men to lift one stack and cart it into the barn. The stack turned out to hold only thirty-two loads. Despite the elder's protests about the compressibility of hay and how it had settled in the stacks, despite his swearing that everything had been done in the fear of God, Levin held his ground: the hay had been divided without his orders, and he would not accept that stack as fifty loads. After a long argument it was settled by the peasants taking the eleven stacks themselves and counting them as fifty loads each. The wrangling and dividing of the haycocks went on the whole afternoon. When the last of the hay had been parceled out, Levin handed the rest of the supervision over to the counting-house clerk and sat down on a haycock marked with a willow stake, looking out admiringly at the meadow swarming with peasants.

In front of him, in a bend of the river beyond the marsh, a bright line of peasant women was moving along, and the scattered hay was being quickly drawn into gray winding rows over the pale green stubble. Behind the women came the men with pitchforks, and out of the gray rows broad, tall, soft haycocks were rising. To the left, carts rumbled over the meadow that had already been cleared, and one after another the haycocks vanished, heaved up in huge forkfuls, and in their place heavy cartloads of fragrant hay rose up, overhanging the horses' hindquarters.

"What weather for haying! What hay this is going to be!" said an old man, squatting down beside Levin. "It's tea, not hay! Look at the way they pick it up — like throwing grain to ducks!" he added, pointing to the growing haycocks. "Since dinner they've carried off a good half of it."
"Last load, is it?" he shouted to a young peasant, who drove past standing on the front of an empty cart, shaking the rope reins.

"The last one, dad!" the boy shouted back as he checked the horse, and, with a grin, he glanced over his shoulder at a bright-cheeked young peasant woman sitting in the cart — who was smiling too — and drove on.
"Who's that? Your son?" Levin asked.
"My baby," said the old man, with a tender smile.
"A fine fellow!"
"The boy's all right."
"Married already?"
"Yes, two years this last St. Philip's day."
"Any children?"
"Children! For over a year he was as innocent as a babe himself — bashful, too," said the old man. "Well, this hay! It's as fragrant as tea!" he repeated, anxious to change the subject.

Levin looked more closely at Ivan Parmenov and his wife. They were loading a haycock onto the cart not far off. Ivan was standing on the cart, taking, settling, and stamping down the huge bundles of hay that his pretty young wife handed up to him with quick, sure movements — first in armfuls, then on the pitchfork. The young wife worked easily, cheerfully, with a deftness that made it look effortless. The packed hay never once tumbled off her fork. First she'd gather it, drive the fork into it, then with a swift, supple motion lean her whole weight on the shaft and at once, with a bend of her back beneath the red sash, draw herself upright, arching her full bosom under the white smock, and with a sharp turn swing the fork around in her arms and pitch the bundle high up onto the cart. Ivan, plainly trying to save her a moment of unnecessary effort wherever he could, hurried — opening his arms wide to catch the bundle and lay it down on the load. As she raked together what was left of the hay, the young wife shook off the bits that had fallen on her neck, straightened the red kerchief that had slipped forward over her white brow — un-browned, unlike her face, by the sun — and ducked under the cart to tie the load down. Ivan showed her how to fasten the cord to the cross-piece, and at something she said he burst out laughing. On both their faces you could see vigorous, young, freshly awakened love.

title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: The load was tied on. Ivan jumped down and took the calm, sleek horse by the bridle. The young wife tossed her rake up onto the load and, with a swinging stride and swinging arms, went to join the women who were forming a circle for the haymakers' dance. Ivan drove out to the road and fell in among the other loaded carts. The peasant women, rakes over their shoulders, bright with wild flowers, chattering in ringing, merry voices, walked behind the hay cart. One wild, untrained female voice broke into song and sang a verse out alone, and then half a hundred strong, healthy voices, coarse and fine all together, picked the verse up and repeated it in unison.

The singing women began to come up close to Levin, and he felt as if a storm of merriment were swooping down on him with a roll of thunder. The storm broke, swallowed him and the haycock where he was lying, and the other haycocks, and the wagonloads, and the whole meadow and the distant fields all seemed to be quaking and singing to the rhythm of this wild happy song with its shouts and whistles and clapping. Levin felt envious of all this health and high spirits; he longed to take part in the expression of this joy of being alive. But there was nothing he could do — he could only lie there, look on, listen. When the peasants had vanished out of sight and hearing with their singing, a weary sense of dejection at his own isolation, his physical idleness, his estrangement from this world, came over him.
