Some of the very peasants who had argued with him most fiercely over the hay, some he had treated harshly, some who had tried to cheat him — those very ones had greeted him good-humoredly, and clearly had not — were incapable of having — any grudge against him, any regret, any memory at all of having tried to deceive him. All of that was drowned in a sea of cheerful shared labor. God gave the day, God gave the strength. And the day and the strength were given over to work, and the work was its own reward. For whom the labor? What would the fruits be? These were idle questions — beside the point.

Levin had often admired this life, had often felt envious of the men who lived it; but today, for the first time — especially under the impression of what he had seen in the way Ivan Parmenov treated his young wife — the thought came to him as a clear possibility that it lay within his power to exchange the dreary, artificial, idle, individualistic life he was leading for this hard-working, pure, and shared life of delight.

The old man who had been sitting beside him had long since gone home; the people had all dispersed. Those who lived nearby had left, while those who had come from a distance had gathered into a group for supper and to spend the night in the meadow. Unnoticed by the peasants, Levin lay on his haycock still, watching, listening, thinking. The peasants who had stayed scarcely slept through the short summer night. At first there was the noise of cheerful talk and laughter all together over supper, then more singing and more laughter.

The whole long day of work had left no mark on them but lightness of heart. Before the first dawn light all was hushed. The only sounds were the night noises of the frogs that never let up in the marsh, and the snorting of the horses through the mist rising over the meadow before morning. Rousing himself, Levin got up from the haycock and, glancing at the stars, saw that night was over.

"Well, what am I to do? How am I to set about it?" he said to himself, trying to put into words all the thoughts and feelings he had passed through during that brief night. All those thoughts and feelings fell into three separate currents. One was the renunciation of his old life, of his entirely useless education. This renunciation gave him satisfaction; it was easy and straightforward. Another current involved the life he longed to lead now. The simplicity, the cleanness, the rightness of that life he could feel clearly, and he was convinced he would find in it the contentment, peace, and dignity whose absence he was so painfully aware of. But a third current circled the question of how to make the transition from the old life to the new. And here nothing took clear shape for him. "Have a wife? Have work, and the necessity of work? Leave Pokrovskoe? Buy land? Join a peasant community? Marry a peasant girl? How am I to set about it?" he asked himself again, and couldn't find an answer. "I haven't slept all night, though, and I can't think it through clearly," he said to himself. "I'll work it out later. One thing's certain: this night has decided my fate. All my old dreams of family life were absurd — not the real thing," he told himself. "It's all much simpler and better than that...."

"How beautiful!" he thought, looking at the strange, almost mother-of-pearl shell of white fleecy cloudlets that lay directly over his head in the middle of the sky. "How exquisite all of this is in this exquisite night! And when was there time for that cloud-shell to form? Only a little while ago I looked at the sky and there was nothing in it — just two white streaks. Yes — and just as imperceptibly my own view of life has shifted!"

He walked out of the meadow and along the highroad toward the village. A slight breeze got up, and the sky turned gray and sullen. The gloomy moment had come that usually precedes the dawn, the full triumph of light over darkness.

Shrinking from the cold, Levin walked quickly, his eyes on the ground. "What's that? Someone coming," he thought, catching the tinkle of bells, and lifting his head. About forty paces off, a carriage with four horses harnessed abreast was coming toward him along the same grassy road. The shaft-horses were being tipped against the shafts by the ruts, but the skilled driver on the box was keeping the shaft clear of them, so that the wheels ran along the smooth part of the road.
That was all Levin took in, and without wondering who it might be, he stared absently at the coach.

Inside it an old lady was dozing in one corner, and at the window, evidently just awake, sat a young girl holding the ribbons of a white cap in both hands. With a face full of light and thought, full of a subtle, intricate inner life that was entirely remote from Levin, she was gazing past him at the glow of the sunrise.
At the very instant when this apparition was about to vanish, the truthful eyes turned and met his. She recognized him, and her face lit up with surprise and joy.

He could not be mistaken. There were no other eyes like those in the world. There was only one being in the world able to gather, for him, all the brightness and meaning of life into a single point. It was she. It was Kitty. He realized she was driving from the railway station out to Ergushovo. And everything that had been working on Levin during that sleepless night, all the resolutions he had made, vanished in an instant. He recalled with a shudder his dreams of marrying a peasant girl. There only — in the carriage that had crossed over to the far side of the road and was rapidly disappearing — there only could he find the solution to the riddle of his life, the riddle that had been weighing so painfully on him lately.

She didn't look out again. The creak of the carriage-springs was no longer audible; the bells could barely be heard. The barking of dogs told him the carriage had reached the village, and what was left was the empty fields all around, the village ahead, and he himself alone, cut off from it all, wandering by himself along the deserted highroad.

He looked up at the sky, expecting to find there the cloud-shell he had been admiring as the emblem of the ideas and feelings of that night. There was nothing in the sky even faintly like a shell. Up there, in the remote heights, a mysterious transformation had taken place. There was no trace of any shell, and what was now stretched over fully half the sky was an even cover of tiny, ever-tinier cloudlets. The sky had turned blue and bright; and with the same softness, the same remoteness, it met his questioning gaze.
"No," he said to himself, "however good that simple life of toil may be, I can't go back to it. I love _her_."

title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: Only those closest to Alexey Alexandrovitch knew that, for all his appearance of being the coldest and most reasonable of men, he had one weakness quite at odds with the general grain of his character. Alexey Alexandrovitch could not hear or see a child or a woman crying without being shaken. The sight of tears threw him into a state of nervous agitation, and he lost any power of clear thought. The chief secretary of his department and his private secretary both knew this, and used to warn women who came in with petitions on no account to let themselves cry, if they didn't want to wreck their chances. "He'll get angry and won't listen to you," they would say. And indeed, in such cases, the emotional disturbance the tears set off in Alexey Alexandrovitch found its outlet in a sudden burst of anger. "There is nothing I can do. Kindly leave the room!" he would normally snap on such occasions.

When Anna, on the drive home from the races, had told him about her relations with Vronsky, and then immediately burst into tears, hiding her face in her hands, Alexey Alexandrovitch, for all the fury raging in him against her, also felt that familiar emotional surge that tears always set off in him. Aware of it, and aware that any show of his feelings at that moment would be entirely out of keeping with the situation, he had tried to suppress every sign of life in himself, and so neither stirred nor looked at her. This was what had produced the strange expression of deathlike rigidity on his face that had struck Anna so forcibly.

When they reached the house he helped her out of the carriage, made an effort to master himself, took leave of her with his customary courtesy, and uttered that phrase that committed him to nothing — saying that tomorrow he would let her know his decision.

His wife's words, which had confirmed his worst suspicions, had driven a cruel pang into Alexey Alexandrovitch's heart. That pang was sharpened by the strange feeling of physical pity for her that her tears had stirred up in him. But once he was alone in the carriage, Alexey Alexandrovitch, to his own surprise and pleasure, felt utterly free both of that pity and of the doubts and torments of jealousy.

It was the sensation of a man who has had a tooth out after suffering for ages from a toothache. After the terrible agony, after the sense of something huge — bigger than his own head — being ripped out of his jaw, the man, hardly able to believe in his own good luck, suddenly realizes that the thing that had been poisoning his life and monopolizing his attention is gone, and that he can live and think again, take an interest in things other than his tooth. This was what Alexey Alexandrovitch was feeling. The agony had been strange and terrible, but it was over; he felt that he could live again and think of something besides his wife.

"No honor, no heart, no religion — a corrupt woman. I always knew it and always saw it, though I tried to deceive myself for her sake," he said to himself. And in fact it now seemed to him that he always had seen it: he ran through episodes from their past in which he had never previously noticed anything wrong — and now those episodes clearly proved she had always been a corrupt woman. "I made a mistake in tying my life to hers; but there was nothing wrong in the mistake itself, and so I cannot be unhappy. It isn't I who am to blame," he told himself, "but she. But I have nothing to do with her. She doesn't exist for me...."

Everything that had to do with her and with their son — toward whom his feelings had shifted as much as toward her — ceased to interest him. The only thing that interested him now was the question of how he could most decently and comfortably (and therefore most justly) extricate himself from the mud she had spattered on him as she fell, and then carry on with his path of active, honorable, and useful work.

"I cannot be made unhappy by the fact that a contemptible woman has committed a crime. I only have to find the best way out of the awkward position she's put me in. And I will find it," he told himself, his frown deepening. "I'm not the first, and I shan't be the last." And, to say nothing of historical examples going all the way back to the "Fair Helen" of Menelaus — recently brought to everyone's memory again — a whole list of contemporary cases of husbands with unfaithful wives in the highest circles rose up before him. "Daryalov, Poltavsky, Prince Karibanov, Count Paskudin, Dram.... Yes, even Dram, that honest, capable fellow... Semyonov, Tchagin, Sigonin," Alexey Alexandrovitch ran through them. "Granted that a certain rather irrational _ridicule_ falls to the lot of these men, still, I never saw it as anything but a misfortune, and always felt sympathy for them," Alexey Alexandrovitch said to himself, though this wasn't true at all: he had never felt sympathy for misfortunes of that kind, and in fact the more often he had heard of unfaithful wives betraying their husbands, the higher his opinion of himself had risen. "It's a misfortune that can fall on anyone. And it has fallen on me. The only thing to be done is to make the best of the position."
And he began going through, point by point, the methods used by men in the same position he was in.
"Daryalov fought a duel...."

The duel had always particularly gripped Alexey Alexandrovitch's imagination in his youth, just because he was physically a coward and knew it perfectly well himself. He couldn't picture without horror the idea of a pistol pointed at him, and he had never in his life so much as handled a weapon. This horror had, in his youth, set him brooding on dueling and picturing himself in situations in which he would have to put his life in danger. Once he had attained success and an established position in the world he had long since forgotten the feeling; but the old groove of feeling reasserted itself, and the dread of his own cowardice proved so strong even now that he spent a long while thinking the question of dueling through from every angle, and dwelling fondly on the idea of a duel, though he knew perfectly well in advance that he would never under any circumstances actually fight one.

"There's no doubt our society is still so barbarous (it's not the same in England) that a great many" — and among these were people whose opinion Alexey Alexandrovitch valued highly — "take a favorable view of the duel; but what does it actually achieve? Suppose I call him out," Alexey Alexandrovitch went on to himself, and, vividly imagining the night he'd spend after issuing the challenge, with the pistol pointed at him, he shuddered and knew that he would never do it — "suppose I call him out. Suppose I get someone to teach me to shoot — I press the trigger," he said to himself, closing his eyes, "and it turns out I've killed him," Alexey Alexandrovitch said to himself, and he shook his head as if to shake away such foolishness. "What sense is there in murdering a man in order to define one's relationship to a guilty wife and son? I would still just as much have to decide what to do with her. And — more probable, and what would almost certainly happen — I'd be killed or wounded. I, the innocent party, would be the victim: killed or wounded. Even more senseless. But beyond that, a challenge to a duel would be a less than honest act on my side. Don't I know perfectly well that my friends would never let me fight one — would never allow the life of a statesman, needed by Russia, to be put at risk? Knowing perfectly well beforehand that the matter would never come to actual danger, the whole business would amount to no more than my trying to win a sham reputation by issuing such a challenge. That would be dishonest, that would be false, that would be self-deception — and the deception of others. A duel is altogether irrational, and nobody expects it of me. My one aim is to protect my reputation, which is essential for the uninterrupted carrying out of my public duties." Official duties, which had always been weighty in Alexey Alexandrovitch's eyes, struck him as especially important at this moment. Having considered and rejected the duel, Alexey Alexandrovitch turned to divorce — another option chosen by several of the husbands he could remember. Running mentally through all the cases of divorce he knew of (and there were plenty in the very highest society, with which he was thoroughly familiar), Alexey Alexandrovitch could not find a single instance in which the object of the divorce was what he had in mind. In all of those cases the husband had practically ceded or sold his unfaithful wife, and the very party who, being at fault, had no right to remarry, had then formed counterfeit, pseudo-marital ties with a self-styled new husband. In his own case, Alexey Alexandrovitch could see that a proper legal divorce — one in which only the guilty wife would be repudiated — was simply unachievable. He saw that the elaborate conditions of the life they led made the coarse proofs of his wife's guilt that the law demanded out of the question; he saw that a certain refinement in that life would not allow such proofs to be brought forward even if he had them, and that to produce them would damage him in public opinion more than it would damage her.

An attempt at divorce could lead to nothing but a public scandal, which would be a godsend to his enemies for slander and attacks on his high standing in society. His main object — to define the situation with as little disturbance as possible — would not be achieved by divorce either. Moreover, in the event of a divorce, or even of an attempt to obtain one, it was obvious that his wife would break off all ties with her husband and throw in her lot with her lover. And in spite of the total contempt and indifference he supposed he felt for his wife, at the bottom of his heart Alexey Alexandrovitch still had one feeling left about her — a reluctance to see her free to throw in her lot with Vronsky, so that her crime would actually have been to her advantage. The mere thought of it so infuriated Alexey Alexandrovitch that the moment it crossed his mind he groaned with inner pain, got up and shifted his place in the carriage, and for a long time after that sat scowling, wrapping his numb, bony legs in the fleecy rug.

"Apart from a formal divorce, one could still do as Karibanov, Paskudin, and that decent fellow Dram did — simply separate from one's wife," he went on, once he had got hold of himself again. But this step too carried the same drawback of public scandal as a divorce; and what was worse, a separation, just like an actual divorce, threw his wife into Vronsky's arms. "No, it's out of the question, out of the question!" he said again, twisting the rug around himself once more. "I cannot be unhappy — but neither she nor he ought to be happy."

The jealousy that had tortured him through the period of uncertainty had dropped away at the instant when the tooth had been wrenched out by his wife's words. But that feeling had been replaced by another — the desire not just that she should fail to be triumphant, but that she should be properly punished for her crime. He didn't acknowledge this feeling to himself, but at the bottom of his heart he longed for her to suffer for having destroyed his peace of mind — his honor. And going once again through the conditions inseparable from a duel, a divorce, a separation, and rejecting each of them again, Alexey Alexandrovitch became convinced that there was only one solution: to keep her with him, hiding what had happened from the world, and using every means in his power to break off the affair — and still more, though he didn't admit this to himself, to punish her. "I must inform her of my conclusion: that, having weighed the terrible position in which she has placed her family, all other solutions will be worse for both sides than the outward _status quo_, and that I am prepared to maintain that status quo, on the strict condition that she obeys my wishes — that is to say, breaks off all communication with her lover." Once this decision had been finally adopted, another weighty consideration occurred to Alexey Alexandrovitch in its favor. "By taking this course alone shall I be acting in accordance with the precepts of religion," he told himself. "In adopting it I am not casting off a guilty wife, but giving her the chance to mend her ways; and, hard as the task will be for me, I shall devote part of my energies to her reform and salvation."

Though Alexey Alexandrovitch knew perfectly well that he could exert no moral influence over his wife, and that any such attempt at reform could lead to nothing but pretense; though in passing through these difficult moments he had not once thought of looking to religion for guidance — now, with his conclusion happening to coincide with what he took to be the requirements of religion, this religious sanction for his decision gave him complete satisfaction and even partly restored his peace of mind. He took pleasure in the thought that, even at such a critical moment in his life, no one would be able to say that he had failed to act on the principles of that religion whose banner he had always held aloft amid the general coolness and indifference. As he turned the matter over and considered what would follow, Alexey Alexandrovitch could not see any reason why his relations with his wife shouldn't carry on practically as before. Of course she could never recover his esteem, but there was, and could be, no reason whatever for his life to be disturbed and for him to suffer because she happened to be a bad and faithless wife. "Yes, time will pass; time, which arranges all things, and the old relations will be restored," Alexey Alexandrovitch told himself; "restored to the extent, that is, that I shall not be conscious of any break in the continuity of my life. She is bound to be unhappy, but I am not at fault, and so I cannot be unhappy."

title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: As he neared Petersburg, Alexey Alexandrovitch was not only sticking firmly to his decision but was even composing in his head the letter he was going to write to his wife. Going into the porter's room, he glanced at the letters and papers that had been brought from his office and instructed that they be taken to him in his study.
"The horses can be unharnessed, and I will see no one," he said in answer to the porter, with a certain pleasure that gave away his agreeable frame of mind as he emphasized the words "see no one."

In his study Alexey Alexandrovitch walked up and down twice and stopped at the huge writing-table, on which the valet who had gone ahead of him had already lit six candles. He cracked his knuckles and sat down, arranging his writing things. Resting his elbows on the table, he tilted his head to one side, thought for a moment, and began to write, without pausing once. He used no form of address to her, and wrote in French, using the plural "_vous_," which doesn't carry the same note of coldness as the corresponding Russian form.

"At our last conversation, I notified you of my intention to communicate to you my decision concerning the subject of that conversation. Having carefully weighed everything, I am writing now in order to keep that promise. My decision is as follows. Whatever your conduct may have been, I do not consider myself entitled to break the bonds in which we have been joined by a Higher Power. The family cannot be broken up by a whim, a caprice, or even by the sin of one of the partners in the marriage, and our life must continue as it has done in the past. This is necessary for me, for you, and for our son. I am fully convinced that you have repented, and do repent, of what has occasioned the present letter, and that you will cooperate with me in rooting out the cause of our estrangement, and in forgetting the past. Otherwise, you can guess what awaits you and your son. All this I hope to discuss in more detail in a personal meeting. As the season is drawing to a close, I would ask you to return to Petersburg as quickly as possible, no later than Tuesday. All necessary preparations will be made for your arrival. I beg you to note that I attach particular importance to compliance with this request.
A. Karenin
"_P.S._ — I enclose the money you may need for your expenses."

He read the letter through and was pleased with it — pleased above all that he had remembered to enclose the money: there wasn't a harsh word in it, no reproach, nor any undue indulgence. Above all, it was a golden bridge home. Folding the letter and smoothing it with a massive ivory paper-knife, slipping it into an envelope with the money, he rang the bell with the satisfaction it always gave him to make use of the well-arranged equipment on his writing-table.
"Give this to the courier to be delivered to Anna Arkadyevna tomorrow at the summer villa," he said, getting up.
"Certainly, your excellency. Tea to be served in the study?"

Alexey Alexandrovitch ordered tea to be brought to the study, and, toying with the heavy paper-knife, moved over to his armchair, beside which had been set out for him a lamp and the French work on Egyptian hieroglyphics he had begun. Over the armchair hung, in a gold frame, an oval portrait of Anna — a fine painting by a celebrated artist. Alexey Alexandrovitch glanced at it. The unfathomable eyes looked back at him ironically and insolently. The black lace about her head, finely caught by the painter, the black hair, the handsome white hand with one finger raised and covered with rings — all of it struck Alexey Alexandrovitch as unbearably insolent and provocative. He stared at the portrait for a minute, then shuddered so violently that his lips quivered and he made a kind of "brrr" sound, and turned away. He hurried over to settle into his armchair and opened the book. He tried to read, but he could not rekindle the lively interest he had previously felt in Egyptian hieroglyphics. He looked at the book and thought about something else. What he was thinking of was not his wife, but a complication that had come up in his official life — at the moment, the main interest there. He felt he had penetrated this tangled affair more deeply than ever before, and that he had hit on a leading idea — he could say this without flattering himself — capable of clearing up the whole business, strengthening his position in his career, putting his enemies on the back foot, and thereby being of the greatest service to the government. The moment the servant had set out the tea and left the room, Alexey Alexandrovitch got up and went to the writing-table. Pulling the portfolio of papers into the middle of the table, with a barely perceptible smile of self-satisfaction, he took a pencil from the rack and plunged into a complicated report on the present complication. The complication was this: Alexey Alexandrovitch's characteristic quality as a politician — that special individual stamp that every rising functionary has, that combination which, along with his unflagging ambition, his reserve, his honesty, and his self-confidence, had made his career — was his contempt for red tape, his cutting down of correspondence, his direct contact, wherever possible, with the living facts, and his economy. It happened that the famous Commission of the 2nd of June had launched an inquiry into the irrigation of land in the Zaraisky province — a matter that fell under Alexey Alexandrovitch's department and that was a glaring instance of fruitless expenditure and paper reforms. Alexey Alexandrovitch knew that this was true. The irrigation of those lands in the Zaraisky province had been initiated by the predecessor of Alexey Alexandrovitch's predecessor. Vast sums had been spent on it, and were still being spent, completely unproductively, and the entire project could plainly lead nowhere. Alexey Alexandrovitch had grasped this as soon as he had taken office, and would have liked to dismantle the Board of Irrigation. But at first, before he yet felt secure in his post, he knew it would touch too many interests and would be impolitic. Later he had been absorbed in other questions and had simply forgotten about the Board of Irrigation. It carried on of its own accord, as such boards do, by sheer inertia. (A great many people made their living out of the Board of Irrigation, especially one highly conscientious and musical family: all the daughters played stringed instruments, and Alexey Alexandrovitch knew the family and had stood godfather to one of the older daughters.) The raising of this question by a hostile department was, in Alexey Alexandrovitch's view, a dishonorable move, given that in every department there were things just like it and worse, into which nobody inquired for well-known reasons of official etiquette. However, now that the gauntlet had been thrown down to him, he had boldly picked it up and demanded the appointment of a special commission to investigate and verify the workings of the Board of Irrigation of the lands in the Zaraisky province. But in return he gave no quarter to the enemy either. He demanded the appointment of another special commission to look into the question of the Native Tribes Organization Committee. The question of the Native Tribes had been raised in passing by the Commission of the 2nd of June, and had been pushed actively by Alexey Alexandrovitch as a matter brooking no delay, given the wretched condition of the native tribes. In the commission this question had become a bone of contention between several departments. The department hostile to Alexey Alexandrovitch insisted that the condition of the native tribes was thriving, that the proposed reorganization might in fact ruin their prosperity, and that if anything was amiss it stemmed mainly from the failure of Alexey Alexandrovitch's department to carry out measures laid down by law. Now Alexey Alexandrovitch intended to demand: first, that a new commission be formed and empowered to investigate the condition of the native tribes on the spot; second, if it should turn out that their condition was actually what it appeared to be from the official documents in the committee's possession, that yet another scientific commission be set up to investigate the wretched condition of the native tribes from the — (1) political, (2) administrative, (3) economic, (4) ethnographic, (5) material, and (6) religious points of view; third, that the rival department be required to produce evidence of the measures it had taken over the last ten years to avert the disastrous conditions in which the native tribes now found themselves; and fourth and finally, that that department explain why it had — as appeared from the evidence before the committee, from Nos. 17,015 and 18,038, from December 5, 1863, and June 7, 1864 — acted in direct contravention of the intent of the law T... Act 18, and the note to Act 36. A flush of eagerness spread over Alexey Alexandrovitch's face as he rapidly wrote out a synopsis of these ideas for his own use. Having filled a sheet of paper, he got up, rang the bell, and sent a note to the chief secretary of his department asking him to look up certain necessary facts. Getting up and pacing about the room, he glanced at the portrait again, frowned, and gave a contemptuous smile. After reading a little more of the book on Egyptian hieroglyphics, and recovering his interest in it, Alexey Alexandrovitch went to bed at eleven o'clock, and as he lay there recalling the incident with his wife, he saw it now in no such gloomy light.

title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: Though Anna had stubbornly and angrily contradicted Vronsky when he told her their position was impossible, deep down she regarded her own position as a lie and a disgrace, and her whole soul ached to change it. On the drive back from the races, in a moment of overwhelm, she had told her husband the truth, and despite the agony it cost her she was glad of it. Once he had left her, she told herself she was glad — that now everything was out in the open and there would be no more lies and pretense. It seemed beyond doubt that her position was now defined once and for all. The new one might be bad, but at least it would be clear; there would be no more uncertainty or falsehood about it. The pain she had inflicted on herself and her husband by speaking those words would be paid back, she thought, in clarity. That evening she saw Vronsky, but she did not tell him what had passed between her and her husband — even though, to make the situation concrete, she would have to.

When she woke up the next morning, the first thing that came back to her were the words she had said to her husband, and they struck her now as so monstrous that she could not imagine how she had brought herself to utter such strange, brutal phrases, and could not imagine what would follow. But the words had been said, and Alexey Alexandrovitch had walked out without saying a thing. "I saw Vronsky and didn't tell him. The very moment he was about to leave I almost called him back to tell him, but I changed my mind, because it was strange that I hadn't told him at once. Why did I want to tell him and then not tell him?" And in answer to that question a burning blush of shame flooded her face. She knew what had stopped her — she knew she had been ashamed. The situation that had seemed so straightforward the night before suddenly looked to her not merely complicated but utterly hopeless. She felt a wave of terror at the disgrace ahead, which she had never even considered before. The instant she pictured what her husband would do, the most horrifying ideas flooded in. She saw herself being turned out of the house, her shame announced to the whole world. She asked herself where she would go once she was out, and could find no answer.

When she thought of Vronsky, it seemed to her that he didn't love her, that he was already beginning to tire of her, that she had no right to offer herself to him — and she felt a sharp resentment against him for it. It seemed to her that the words she had spoken to her husband, and had been turning over and over in her mind, she had spoken to everyone, and that everyone had heard them. She couldn't bring herself to look the people of her own household in the face. She couldn't bring herself to call her maid, much less go downstairs and face her son and his governess.

The maid, who had been listening at her door for some time, came in on her own initiative. Anna shot her a questioning look and blushed in alarm. The maid apologized for coming in, saying she had thought she heard the bell. She brought in clothes and a note. The note was from Betsy. Betsy reminded her that Liza Merkalova and Baroness Shtoltz were coming over that morning to play croquet, with their admirers Kaluzhsky and old Stremov. "Come, if only as a study in social morals. I'll expect you," she finished.
Anna read the note and let out a deep sigh.
"Nothing, I don't need anything," she said to Annushka, who was rearranging the bottles and brushes on the dressing table. "You can go. I'll dress in a minute and come down. I don't need anything."

Annushka went out, but Anna did not start dressing — she stayed in the same posture, head and hands hanging limp, and every now and then she shuddered all over, seemed about to make some gesture or say something, and then sank back into stillness. She kept repeating, "My God, my God!" — but neither the "God" nor the "my" meant anything to her. The thought of turning to religion for help in her trouble was as remote from her as turning to Alexey Alexandrovitch himself, even though she had never doubted the faith in which she had been raised. She knew that religion's support was available only on condition of giving up the very thing that gave her life its whole meaning. She was not merely miserable — she was beginning to feel a real alarm at this new state of mind, one she had never experienced before. It was as if everything in her soul were doubling, the way objects sometimes appear double to exhausted eyes. At times she barely knew what she dreaded and what she hoped for. Whether she dreaded or longed for what had already happened, or what was about to happen, and what exactly she wanted — she could not have said.

"Oh, what am I doing!" she said to herself, suddenly feeling a stab of pain on both sides of her head. When she came to, she found she was clutching her hair at the temples with both hands, pulling at it. She jumped up and started pacing.
"The coffee is ready, and mademoiselle and Seryozha are waiting," said Annushka, coming back in and finding Anna in the same position.
"Seryozha? What about Seryozha?" Anna asked, suddenly eager, remembering for the first time that morning that her son existed.
"He's been naughty, I think," Annushka answered with a smile.
"How so?"
"There were some peaches sitting on the table in the corner room. I think he sneaked in and ate one when no one was looking."

The thought of her son suddenly pulled Anna out of the helpless state she'd been in. She remembered the partly genuine, though heavily exaggerated, role she had taken on over the past few years — the mother who lives for her child — and she felt a rush of joy at realizing that in this mess she had a foothold quite independent of her relations with her husband or Vronsky. That foothold was her son. Whatever her position turned out to be, she could not lose her son. Her husband might humiliate her and throw her out, Vronsky might cool toward her and go on with his own separate life (she thought of him again with bitterness and reproach) — she could not abandon her son. She had a purpose. And she had to act — act to lock in this connection with her son, so that he wouldn't be taken from her. Quickly, as fast as humanly possible, she had to act before they took him away. She had to take her son and leave. That was the one thing she had to do now. She needed consolation. She had to be calm and find a way out of this unbearable position. The thought of immediate action that would bind her to her son, of going off somewhere with him, was the consolation she found.

She dressed quickly, went downstairs, and with firm steps walked into the drawing room, where as usual she found coffee, Seryozha, and his governess waiting for her. Seryozha, dressed all in white, was bent over a table under a mirror, his back and head curved with that look of intense concentration she knew well — the one that made him resemble his father — fussing with some flowers in his hand.

The governess had a particularly stern expression. Seryozha shrieked in his usual high pitch, "Oh, mamma!" and then stopped, uncertain whether to come and greet his mother and set the flowers down, or to finish the wreath first and bring the flowers with him.

After saying good morning, the governess launched into a long, detailed account of Seryozha's bad behavior, but Anna did not hear her — she was busy weighing whether or not to take the governess with her. "No, I won't take her," she decided. "I'll go alone with my child."

"Yes, it was very wrong," said Anna, and taking her son by the shoulder she looked at him — not sternly, but with a timid look that left the boy both confused and thrilled — and kissed him. "Leave him with me," she said to the startled governess, and without letting go of her son she sat down at the table where her coffee had been set out.
"Mamma! I... I... didn't...," he said, trying to read her face for some hint of what was coming on the peach question.
"Seryozha," she said, as soon as the governess had left the room, "that was wrong, but you'll never do it again, will you? You love me?"

She felt tears welling up. "How can I help loving him?" she said to herself, looking deep into his frightened and at the same time delighted eyes. "And could he ever side with his father against me? Could he really not feel for me?" Tears were already running down her face, and to hide them she got up abruptly and almost ran out onto the terrace.
After the days of thunderstorms, cold, bright weather had set in. The air was cool in the bright sun that filtered through the freshly washed leaves.
She shivered — partly from the cold, partly from the inward horror that had taken hold of her again in the open air.

"Run along, run along to Mariette," she said to Seryozha, who had followed her out, and she began pacing up and down the straw matting of the terrace. "Can it really be that they won't forgive me, won't understand that none of this could have been helped?" she said to herself.

Standing still and looking up at the tops of the aspens swaying in the wind, their freshly washed leaves glinting in the cold sunshine, she knew that they would not forgive her — that everyone and everything would now be as merciless to her as that sky, that green. And once again she felt her soul splitting in two. "I mustn't, mustn't think," she said to herself. "I have to get ready. To go where? When? Whom to take? Yes — to Moscow on the evening train. Annushka and Seryozha, and only the bare essentials. But first I have to write to them both." She walked briskly back inside to her boudoir, sat down at the table, and wrote to her husband: "After what has happened, I cannot stay any longer in your house. I am leaving and taking my son with me. I don't know the law and so I don't know which of the parents the son should remain with; but I am taking him with me because I cannot live without him. Be generous and leave him to me."

Up to this point she wrote rapidly and freely, but the appeal to a generosity she did not recognize in him, and the need to round off the letter with something moving, brought her up short. "Of my fault and my remorse I cannot speak, because..."

She stopped again, unable to connect the thought. "No," she said to herself, "there's no need for any of this," and tearing up the letter she wrote it again, leaving out the line about generosity, and sealed it.

Another letter had to go to Vronsky. "I have told my husband," she wrote — and then sat for a long time unable to add anything more. It was so coarse, so unwomanly. "And what else am I supposed to write to him?" she said to herself. Again a flush of shame swept over her face; she remembered his composure, and a wave of anger at him drove her to tear the sheet with that one phrase into tiny scraps. "No need for anything," she said to herself, and closing her blotting-case she went upstairs, told the governess and the servants that she was leaving for Moscow that day, and at once set to work packing her things.

title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: Every room of the summer villa was full of porters, gardeners, and footmen carrying things back and forth. Cupboards and chests stood open; twice they had sent to the shop for more cord; sheets of newspaper were strewn across the floor. Two trunks, several bags, and some strapped-up rugs had been carried down into the hall. The carriage and two hired cabs were waiting at the steps. Anna, forgetting her own inner turmoil in the work of packing, was standing at a table in her boudoir loading her travel bag when Annushka drew her attention to the sound of a carriage pulling up. Anna looked out of the window and saw Alexey Alexandrovitch's courier on the steps, ringing the bell.

"Go and find out what it is," she said, and with a calm sense of being prepared for anything she sat down in a low chair, folded her hands on her knees. A footman brought in a thick packet addressed in Alexey Alexandrovitch's hand.
"The courier has been told to wait for an answer," he said.

"Very well," she said, and the moment he had left the room she tore the letter open with trembling fingers. A roll of unfolded banknotes wrapped in paper dropped out of it. She pulled out the letter and started reading it from the end. "Arrangements will be made for your arrival here... I attach particular importance to compliance..." she read. She ran forward, then back, read it through, then read it again from the beginning. By the time she finished, she felt cold all over, with the sense that some terrible disaster, beyond anything she had imagined, had just crashed down on her.

That morning she had regretted speaking to her husband and wanted nothing more than to be able to take those words back. And here was this letter treating them as unspoken and giving her exactly what she had wanted. But now the letter struck her as more dreadful than anything she could have imagined.

"He's right!" she said. "Of course he's right — he's always right; he's a Christian, he's generous! Yes — vile, low creature! And no one sees it but me, and no one ever will; and I can't explain it. They say he's so religious, so high-minded, so honest, so clever — but they don't see what I've seen. They don't know how he has crushed my life for eight years, crushed everything alive in me — not once has it occurred to him that I'm a living woman who needs love. They don't know how at every step he has humiliated me, while feeling perfectly pleased with himself. Haven't I tried, tried with everything in me, to find something to give my life meaning? Haven't I struggled to love him, to love my son when I couldn't love my husband? But the time came when I knew I couldn't fool myself any longer, that I was alive, that I wasn't to blame, that God has made me so that I have to love and to live. And now what does he do? If he had killed me, if he had killed him, I could have borne anything, I could have forgiven anything. But no — he... How did I not see what he would do? He's doing exactly what suits his mean character. He'll keep himself in the right, while me, ruined as I am, he'll drive lower still, into worse ruin..."

She remembered the words from the letter. "You can imagine what awaits you and your son..." "That's a threat to take my child away, and most likely under their idiotic laws he can do it. But I know perfectly well why he writes that. He doesn't believe even in my love for my child — or he despises it (the way he always used to mock it). He despises that feeling in me, but he knows I won't abandon my child, that I can't abandon my child, that there could be no life for me without my child, even with the man I love; but that if I did abandon my child and run off with him, I would be behaving like the basest, most disgraceful of women. He knows that, and he knows I'm not capable of it."

She remembered another sentence from the letter. "Our life must go on as before..." "That life was wretched enough in the old days; it has been unbearable lately. What will it be now? And he knows all that — he knows that I cannot repent of breathing, of loving; he knows it can only lead to lying and deceit; but he wants to keep on torturing me. I know him — I know that lies are his element, that he's at home and happy in them, like a fish in water. No — I won't give him that happiness. I'll tear through this spiderweb of lies he's trying to catch me in, whatever it costs. Anything is better than lying and pretense."
"But how? Oh God, oh God! Was there ever a woman as wretched as I am?..."

"No — I will break through it, I will break through it!" she cried, jumping up and forcing back her tears. And she went to the writing-table to write him another letter. But at the bottom of her heart she felt she was not strong enough to break through anything — not strong enough to get out of her old position, however false and shameful it might be.

She sat down at the writing-table, but instead of writing she clasped her hands on the table, dropped her head onto them, and burst into tears with sobs and a heaving chest, like a child crying. She was weeping because her dream of having her position made clear and definite had been wiped out forever. She knew in advance that everything would go on as before — and in fact far worse than before. She felt that her place in society, which had seemed so trivial to her that morning, was actually precious to her — that she wouldn't have the strength to exchange it for the disgraceful position of a woman who has abandoned her husband and child to join her lover; that struggle as she might, she could not be stronger than herself. She would never know freedom in love; she would remain forever a guilty wife, with the threat of exposure hanging over her at every moment, deceiving her husband for the sake of a shameful affair with a man living his own life apart from hers, a life she could never share. She knew that was how it would be — and yet it was so awful that she couldn't even picture how it would end. And she cried unrestrainedly, the way children cry when they're punished.
The sound of the footman's steps forced her to pull herself together, and, hiding her face from him, she pretended to be writing.
"The courier is asking whether there's an answer," the footman announced.
"An answer? Yes," said Anna. "Tell him to wait. I'll ring."

"What can I write?" she thought. "What can I decide on my own? What do I know? What do I want? What do I even care about?" Again she felt her soul splitting in two. The feeling terrified her, and she grabbed at the first pretext for doing something that might pull her thoughts off herself. "I have to see Alexey" (that was what she called Vronsky to herself); "no one but he can tell me what I should do. I'll go to Betsy's; maybe I'll see him there," she said to herself, completely forgetting that when she had told him the day before she wasn't going to Princess Tverskaya's, he had said in that case he wouldn't go either. She went over to the table, wrote to her husband, "I have received your letter. — A."; then she rang and gave it to the footman.
"We're not going," she said to Annushka as she came in.
"Not going at all?"
"No; don't unpack until tomorrow, and have the carriage wait. I'm going to the princess's."
"Which dress shall I get ready?"

title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The croquet party Princess Tverskaya had invited Anna to was to consist of two ladies and their admirers. The two ladies were the leading figures of a select new Petersburg circle, nicknamed in imitation of some imitation _les sept merveilles du monde_. These ladies belonged to a set that, while of the very highest society, was thoroughly hostile to the one Anna moved in. On top of that, Stremov, one of the most influential men in Petersburg and the elderly admirer of Liza Merkalova, was Alexey Alexandrovitch's enemy in the political world. All of which meant Anna had not intended to go, and the hints in Princess Tverskaya's note referred to that refusal. But now Anna was eager to go, in the hope of seeing Vronsky.
Anna arrived at Princess Tverskaya's earlier than the other guests.

At the same moment she entered, Vronsky's footman, with side-whiskers combed out like a _Kammerjunker_, came in too. He stopped at the door, took off his cap, and let her pass. Anna recognized him, and only then remembered that Vronsky had told her the day before he wouldn't be coming. He was probably sending a note to that effect.
As she took off her wrap in the hall, she heard the footman — rolling his _r's_ like a _Kammerjunker_ — say, "From the count for the princess," and hand the note over.

She longed to ask him where his master was. She longed to turn back and send him with a letter telling Vronsky to come to her, or to go and see him herself. But none of these three options was possible. The bells were already ringing to announce her arrival further inside, and Princess Tverskaya's footman was standing at the open door waiting for her to walk through into the inner rooms.
"The princess is in the garden; they will let her know at once. Would you like to walk out into the garden?" announced another footman in another room.

The state of uncertainty, of being unable to decide, was just the same as at home — worse, in fact, since here she couldn't take any step, couldn't see Vronsky, and had to stay among strangers, in company so out of step with her present mood. But she was wearing a dress she knew suited her. She wasn't alone; the whole familiar luxurious setting of idleness was around her, and she felt less miserable here than at home. She wasn't being forced to think about what to do next. Things would happen of their own accord. When she met Betsy coming toward her in a white gown whose elegance struck her, Anna smiled at her exactly as she always did. Princess Tverskaya was walking with Tushkevitch and a young lady — a relative who, to the great delight of her parents back in the provinces, was spending the summer with the fashionable princess.
There was clearly something unusual about Anna, because Betsy noticed it immediately.
"I slept badly," Anna answered, looking hard at the footman coming toward them — the one, she supposed, bringing Vronsky's note.

"I'm so glad you've come!" said Betsy. "I'm tired and was just longing for some tea before they arrive. You go off" — she turned to Tushkevitch — "with Masha and try out the croquet ground over there, where they've been cutting it. We'll have time to talk a little over tea; we'll have a cozy chat, eh?" she said to Anna in English with a smile, squeezing the hand that held her parasol.

"Yes, especially since I can't stay with you very long. I have to go on to old Madame Vrede. I've been promising for ages," said Anna — and for her, lying, foreign as it was to her nature, had become not merely easy and natural in society but a positive source of pleasure. Why she said this, when it hadn't crossed her mind a second earlier, she could not have explained. She had said it simply on the reflection that since Vronsky wouldn't be here she had better secure her freedom and try to see him somehow. But why she had picked old Madame Vrede, whom she did indeed need to visit — as she had to visit any number of other people — she could not have explained; and yet, as it turned out later, if she had tried to invent the most cunning device for meeting Vronsky, she could not have come up with anything better.

"No. I won't let you go on any account," Betsy answered, looking keenly into Anna's face. "Honestly, if I weren't fond of you, I'd be offended. You'd think you were afraid my company would compromise you. Tea in the little dining room, please," she said, half closing her eyes as she always did when speaking to a footman.
Taking the note from him, she read it.

"Alexey is letting us down," she said in French; "he writes that he can't come," she added in a tone so simple and natural that it could never have occurred to her Vronsky might mean anything more to Anna than a game of croquet. Anna knew Betsy knew everything — but hearing the way she spoke of Vronsky in front of her, she was almost convinced for a moment that Betsy knew nothing.
"Ah!" said Anna, indifferent, as though she had no real interest in the matter, and she went on smiling: "How could you or your friends compromise anyone?"

This playing with words, this hiding of a secret, had a great fascination for Anna, as it does for all women. And it wasn't the necessity of concealment, nor the purpose the concealment served, but the act of concealing itself that drew her in.

"I can't be more Catholic than the Pope," she said. "Stremov and Liza Merkalova — they're the cream of the cream of society. And anyway, they're received everywhere, and _I_" — she put special emphasis on the I — "have never been strict or intolerant. I simply don't have the time."

"No, you don't care, perhaps, about meeting Stremov? Let him and Alexey Alexandrovitch tilt at each other in committee — that's no business of ours. But in society he's the most pleasant man I know, and a devoted croquet player. You'll see. And in spite of his ridiculous position as Liza's lovesick admirer at his age, you have to see how he carries the absurdity off. He's very charming. Sappho Shtoltz you don't know? Oh, that's a new type, quite new."

Betsy said all this, and at the same time, from her good-humored, shrewd glance, Anna sensed that she had partly guessed at her situation and was hatching something on her behalf. They were in the little boudoir.
"I'd better write to Alexey, though," and Betsy sat down at the table, scribbled a few lines, and put the note in an envelope.

"I'm telling him to come to dinner. I've got one extra lady to dinner and no man to take her in. Look at what I've said — will that persuade him? Excuse me, I have to leave you a minute. Would you seal it up and send it off? I have to give some orders," she said from the doorway.

Without a second's thought, Anna sat down at the table with Betsy's letter, and without even reading it she wrote underneath: "I must see you. Come to the garden at the Vredes'. I shall be there at six." She sealed it, and when Betsy came back, handed the note to be taken right in front of her.

At tea, brought to them on a little table in the cool little drawing room, the cozy chat Princess Tverskaya had promised before the arrival of her guests really did materialize between the two women. They picked over the people they were expecting, and the talk fell on Liza Merkalova.
"She's very sweet, and I always liked her," said Anna.

"You should like her. She raves about you. Yesterday she came up to me after the races, desperate not to find you. She says you're a real heroine out of a novel, and that if she were a man she'd do any number of mad things for you. Stremov says she does that as it is."

"But do tell me, please — I never could make it out," said Anna after a silence, in a tone that showed she wasn't just making conversation but that the question mattered to her more than it ought to. "Do tell me, please — what is the actual relationship between her and Prince Kaluzhsky, the one they call Mishka? I've seen so little of them. What does it mean?"
Betsy smiled with her eyes and looked at Anna intently.
"It's a new manner," she said. "They've all taken to it. They've flung their caps over the windmill. But there are different ways of flinging it."
"Yes, but what are her relations with Kaluzhsky, exactly?"
Betsy burst into peals of unexpectedly merry, irrepressible laughter, something that rarely happened with her.

"You're trespassing on Princess Myakaya's special territory now. That's the question of an _enfant terrible_," — and Betsy obviously tried to hold herself back, but couldn't, and went off into the kind of contagious laughter that comes out of people who don't laugh often. "You'd better ask them," she got out between tears of laughter.
"No — you laugh," said Anna, laughing in spite of herself, "but I never could understand it. I can't understand the husband's role in it."

"The husband? Liza Merkalova's husband carries her shawl and stands ready to make himself useful. Anything more than that, no one cares to inquire too closely. You know in decent society one doesn't talk or even think about certain details of dress. It's the same with this."
"Will you be at Madame Rolandak's fête?" Anna asked, changing the subject.

"I don't think so," Betsy answered, and without looking at her friend she began filling the little translucent cups with fragrant tea. Setting a cup in front of Anna, she took out a cigarette, fitted it into a silver holder, and lit it.

"It's like this, you see — I'm in a fortunate position," she began, fully serious now as she picked up her cup. "I understand you, and I understand Liza. Liza is one of those naive natures that, like children, simply don't know what's good and what's bad. At any rate, she didn't grasp it when she was very young. And now she's aware that the not-grasping suits her. Now, perhaps, she doesn't grasp on purpose," Betsy said with a subtle smile. "But either way it suits her. The same thing, you see, can be looked at tragically and turned into agony, or it can be looked at simply and even humorously. You may be inclined to look at it all too tragically."
"How I wish I knew other people the way I know myself!" said Anna, in a serious, dreamy voice. "Am I worse than other people, or better? I think I'm worse."
"_Enfant terrible, enfant terrible!_" Betsy repeated. "But here they are."

title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: They heard the sound of footsteps and a man's voice, then a woman's voice and laughter, and right after that the expected guests walked in: Sappho Shtoltz, and a young man brimming with excess health, the so-called Vaska. It was clear that ample supplies of beefsteak, truffles, and Burgundy never failed to reach him on schedule. Vaska bowed to the two ladies and glanced at them, but only for an instant. He followed Sappho into the drawing room, sticking close as if chained to her, his glittering eyes fixed on her as if he meant to devour her. Sappho Shtoltz was a blonde beauty with black eyes. She moved in brisk little steps in high-heeled shoes and shook the ladies' hands as vigorously as a man would.

Anna had never met this new star of fashion before, and was struck by her looks, the extreme to which her dress was carried, and the boldness of her manner. On her head was such a tower of soft golden hair — part her own, part false — that her head was equal in scale to the elegantly rounded bust, of which a great deal was on display in front. The impulsive abruptness of her movements was such that with every step the lines of her knees and the upper part of her legs showed distinctly through her dress, and the question came to mind, against one's will, where the actual body of the woman — so small and slender, so bare in front, so hidden behind and below — really ended within that undulating, piled-up mountain of fabric at the back.
Betsy hurried to introduce her to Anna.

"Just imagine — we almost ran over two soldiers," she began telling them right away, working her eyes, smiling, and flicking back her train with a single sweep to one side. "I drove here with Vaska... Oh, that's right, you don't know each other." And mentioning his surname she introduced the young man, then, blushing a little, broke into a ringing laugh at her own mistake — at having used "Vaska" in front of a stranger. Vaska bowed to Anna again but said nothing to her. He turned to Sappho: "You've lost your bet. We got here first. Pay up," he said, smiling.
Sappho laughed even more brightly.
"Not just now," she said.
"Oh, fine, later then."

"All right, all right. Oh — yes!" She turned abruptly to Princess Betsy. "I'm a charming person, you know... I completely forgot. I've brought you a visitor. And here he comes." The unexpected young visitor Sappho had invited and then forgotten was, however, a person of such consequence that, in spite of his youth, both ladies got to their feet at his entrance.
He was Sappho's newest admirer. He now trailed her like Vaska.

Soon after, Prince Kaluzhsky arrived, and then Liza Merkalova with Stremov. Liza Merkalova was a thin brunette with an Oriental, languid type of face and — as everyone always said — exquisite, enigmatic eyes. The tone of her dark dress (Anna noticed and appreciated this at once) matched her style of beauty perfectly. Liza was as soft and languid as Sappho was brisk and abrupt.

But to Anna's taste, Liza was far more attractive. Betsy had told Anna that Liza had adopted the pose of an innocent child, but when Anna actually saw her she felt that wasn't quite the truth. She really was both innocent and corrupt at once, but sweet and passive. It was true that her tone was the same as Sappho's; that, like Sappho, she had two men, one young and one old, tacked on to her, devouring her with their eyes. But there was something in her that rose above what surrounded her. There was in her the glow of a real diamond among glass imitations. That glow shone out in her exquisite, truly enigmatic eyes. The weary, and at the same time passionate, look of those eyes, ringed with dark shadows, struck one by its perfect sincerity. Anyone looking into them imagined he knew her completely, and that knowing her, he could not but love her. At the sight of Anna, her whole face lit up at once with a smile of delight.

"Ah, how glad I am to see you!" she said, going up to her. "At the races yesterday all I wanted was to reach you, but you had gone. I really wanted to see you yesterday especially. Wasn't it dreadful?" she said, looking at Anna with eyes that seemed to lay her whole soul bare.
"Yes — I had no idea it would be so wrenching," said Anna, blushing.
At that moment the company got up to go into the garden.
"I'm not going," said Liza, smiling and settling herself close to Anna. "You won't go either, will you? Who wants to play croquet?"
"Oh, I enjoy it," said Anna.
"How is it you never get bored by anything? It's a delight just to look at you. You're alive — and I'm bored."
"How can you be bored? You live in the liveliest set in Petersburg," said Anna.
"Possibly the people not in our set are even more bored; but we — I, certainly — aren't happy. We're hideously, hideously bored."
Sappho, lighting a cigarette, went off into the garden with the two young men. Betsy and Stremov stayed at the tea-table.
"What — bored!" said Betsy. "Sappho says they had a marvelous time at your place last night."

"Ugh, how dismal it all was!" said Liza Merkalova. "We all drove back to my place after the races. And always the same people, always the same. Always the same thing. We lounged about on sofas the whole evening. What's there to enjoy in that? No — do tell me how you manage never to be bored?" she said, turning back to Anna. "One look at you and one sees, here's a woman who might be happy or unhappy, but isn't bored. Tell me how you do it?"
"I do nothing," Anna answered, blushing at this probing.

"That's the best method," Stremov put in. Stremov was a man of fifty, partly gray, still vigorous-looking, very ugly but with a distinctive, intelligent face. Liza Merkalova was his wife's niece, and he spent all his free hours with her. On meeting Anna Karenina — being, as he was, Alexey Alexandrovitch's enemy in government — he tried, like a shrewd man of the world, to be especially courteous to her, the wife of his enemy.

"'Nothing,'" he put in with a subtle smile, "that's the very best method. I told you long ago," he said, turning to Liza Merkalova, "that if you don't want to be bored, you mustn't think you're going to be bored. It's just the same as not being able to fall asleep when you're afraid of not being able to fall asleep. That's exactly what Anna Arkadyevna just said."
"I'd be very pleased if I had said it, because it's not only clever but also true," said Anna, smiling.
"No — do tell me, why is it one can't go to sleep, and one can't help being bored?"
"To sleep well one has to work, and to enjoy oneself one has to work too."
"And what am I supposed to work for, when my work is no use to anyone? I can't and won't deliberately fake it."

"You're incorrigible," said Stremov, not looking at her, and he turned back to Anna. Since he rarely met Anna, he could only say commonplaces — but he said those commonplaces, about when she was returning to Petersburg and how fond Countess Lidia Ivanovna was of her, in a tone that suggested he longed with his whole soul to please her, to show his regard for her, and even more than that.
Tushkevitch came in to announce that the others were waiting for the rest of the players to begin croquet.
"No, don't go, please don't," pleaded Liza Merkalova, hearing that Anna was going to leave. Stremov joined her appeals.

"It's too violent a transition," he said, "to go from this kind of company to old Madame Vrede. And besides, you'll only give her an opening for scandal-mongering, while here you stir nothing but very different feelings — feelings of the highest and most opposite kind," he said to her.

Anna paused for a moment, weighing it. This shrewd man's flattering words, the naive, childlike affection Liza Merkalova was showing her, the whole familiar social atmosphere — it was all so easy, and what lay ahead of her was so hard, that for a moment she hesitated whether to stay, whether to put off the painful moment of explanation a little longer. But remembering what was waiting for her alone at home, if she didn't come to some decision — remembering that gesture, terrible even in memory, when she had clutched her hair in both hands — she said goodbye and left.

title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: In spite of Vronsky's seemingly frivolous social life, he was a man who hated disorder. Early on, as a youth in the Corps of Pages, he had once experienced the humiliation of a refusal when, in a tight spot, he had tried to borrow money — and since then he had never put himself in that position again.

To keep his affairs in some kind of order, he used about five times a year (more or less often, depending on circumstances) to shut himself up alone and put everything into clear shape. He called this his day of reckoning, or _faire la lessive_.

Waking up the day after the races, Vronsky put on a white linen coat, and without shaving or taking a bath he spread his money, bills, and letters across the table and got to work. Petritsky, who knew he was in a foul mood on these occasions, woke up, saw his comrade at the writing-table, and dressed and slipped out quietly without getting in his way.

Every man who knows in minute detail the full complexity of the conditions he is surrounded by cannot help imagining that this complexity, and the difficulty of sorting it out, is something exceptional and personal — peculiar to himself — and never suspects that everyone else is surrounded by an equally tangled set of personal affairs. So it seemed to Vronsky. And not without some inner pride, and not without reason, he thought that any other man would long ago have come to grief or been forced into something dishonorable if he had found himself in such a tight position. But Vronsky felt that right now in particular it was essential to clarify and define his position if he wanted to avoid getting into trouble.

What Vronsky tackled first, as the easiest, was his money. Writing out all his debts on notepaper in his small hand, he added them up and found that they came to seventeen thousand and some odd hundreds, which he left off for the sake of clarity. Counting up his cash and his bank book, he found he had one thousand eight hundred roubles left, with nothing coming in before the New Year. Going over the list of debts again, Vronsky copied it out, sorting them into three classes. In the first class he put the debts that had to be paid at once, or for which he had to have the money ready so there could be no delay if payment were demanded. These came to about four thousand: one thousand five hundred for a horse, and two thousand five hundred as surety for a younger comrade, Venovsky, who had lost that sum to a cardsharper in Vronsky's presence. Vronsky had wanted to pay the money at the time (he had had the amount then), but Venovsky and Yashvin had insisted that they would pay, not Vronsky, who hadn't played. That much was all right, but Vronsky knew that in this dirty business — even though his only stake in it was a verbal promise to be Venovsky's surety — it was essential to have the two thousand five hundred roubles, so he could fling it at the swindler and have no more dealings with him. So for this first and most important category he needed four thousand roubles. The second class — eight thousand roubles — consisted of less urgent debts. These were mostly accounts connected with his race horses: the dealer in oats and hay, the English saddler, and so on. He would need to pay about two thousand roubles on those debts too in order to be quite free of worry. The last class of debts — to shops, to hotels, to his tailor — were not worth thinking about. So he needed at least six thousand roubles for current expenses, and he had only one thousand eight hundred. For a man with an income of one hundred thousand roubles, which was what everyone took Vronsky's income to be, debts like these should hardly have been embarrassing — but the truth was he was far from having one hundred thousand. His father's enormous fortune, which alone produced two hundred thousand a year, was still left undivided between the brothers. When the elder brother, weighed down with debts, had married Princess Varya Tchirkova, the penniless daughter of a Decembrist, Alexey had given up to his elder brother nearly the whole income from his father's estate, reserving for himself only twenty-five thousand a year out of it. Alexey had said to his brother at the time that this would be enough for him until he married — which he probably never would. And his brother, who commanded one of the most expensive regiments and had only just been married, could not refuse the gift. His mother, who had her own separate fortune, had been adding another twenty thousand a year to the twenty-five he had set aside, and Alexey had spent it all. Lately his mother, furious with him over his love affair and his leaving Moscow, had stopped sending him the money. As a result, Vronsky — who was used to a scale of forty-five thousand a year and had only received twenty thousand that year — found himself in trouble. He could not turn to his mother to get out of it. Her latest letter, received the day before, had especially infuriated him with its hints that she was perfectly ready to help him succeed in society and in the army, but not to support a life that was a scandal to all of decent society. His mother's attempt to buy him cut him to the quick and made him feel colder to her than ever. But he couldn't go back on the generous gesture once it had been made — even though he now felt, vaguely sensing certain possibilities ahead in his affair with Madame Karenina, that the generous gesture had been made carelessly, and that even unmarried he might need all hundred thousand of the income. But he couldn't undo it. He only had to remember his brother's wife, to remember how that dear, sweet Varya took every chance to remind him that she remembered his generosity and was grateful for it, to feel that taking the gift back was out of the question. It was as impossible as beating a woman, stealing, or lying. One thing only could and ought to be done, and Vronsky decided on it without an instant's hesitation: to borrow money from a money-lender — ten thousand roubles, a thing that presented no difficulty — to cut back his expenses across the board, and to sell his race horses. Having decided this, he immediately wrote a note to Rolandak, who had sent more than once with offers to buy horses from him. Then he sent for the Englishman and the money-lender, and divided what cash he had according to the bills he meant to pay. With that finished, he wrote a cold and cutting reply to his mother. Then he took out three notes from Anna out of his notebook, read them through again, burned them, and remembering their conversation the day before, sank into thought.

title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Vronsky's life was particularly happy in this: he had a code of principles that laid down with unfailing certainty what he ought and ought not to do. The code covered only a very small range of situations, but within that range the principles were never in doubt, and Vronsky, who never stepped outside it, had never had a moment's hesitation about doing what he was supposed to do. The principles laid down as fixed rules: that one must pay a card-sharper but need not pay one's tailor; that one must never lie to a man but may lie to a woman; that one must never cheat anyone but may cheat a husband; that one must never forgive an insult but may give one — and so on. These principles might not be reasonable or good, but they were unfailingly certain, and as long as he kept to them Vronsky felt that his heart was at peace and his head could stay up. Only quite recently, in connection with his affair with Anna, had Vronsky begun to feel that his code didn't fully cover every possible case, and to foresee in the future difficulties and dilemmas for which he could find no clear guide.
His present relation to Anna and to her husband seemed to him clear and simple. It was clearly and precisely defined in the code he lived by.

She was an honorable woman who had given him her love, and he loved her, and so in his eyes she was a woman entitled to the same respect as a lawful wife, or more. He would have had his hand cut off before he allowed himself by a word, by even a hint, to humiliate her, or to fall short of the fullest respect any woman could expect.

His attitude toward society was clear as well. Anyone might know, anyone might suspect — but no one was to dare speak of it. If anyone did, he was ready to force every speaker to be silent and to respect the nonexistent honor of the woman he loved.

His attitude toward the husband was the clearest of all. From the moment Anna had loved Vronsky, he had regarded his own right over her as the one thing beyond question. The husband was simply a superfluous, tiresome presence. No doubt the man was in a pitiable position — but how could that be helped? The one right the husband had was to demand satisfaction with a weapon in his hand, and Vronsky was prepared for that at any moment.

But lately a new kind of inner connection had grown up between him and her, one whose vagueness frightened Vronsky. Only the day before she had told him she was pregnant. And he felt that this fact, and what she expected of him in response to it, called for something not fully spelled out in the code by which he had so far steered his life. He had indeed been caught off guard, and in the first moment when she spoke to him about her position, his heart had urged him to beg her to leave her husband. He had said it — but now, thinking it over, he saw clearly that it would be better to find a way to avoid that; and at the same time, even as he was telling himself this, he was afraid it might be wrong.

"If I told her to leave her husband, that would mean joining her life to mine; am I ready for that? How am I supposed to take her away now, with no money? Suppose I could arrange it... But how can I take her away while I'm still in the service? If I say it — I have to be prepared to do it, that is, I have to have the money and to retire from the army."
And he fell into thought. The question of whether to retire from the service or not led him to the other and perhaps the chief, though hidden, interest of his life — one no one but he knew about.

Ambition was the old dream of his youth and childhood, a dream he didn't even admit to himself, although it was so strong that this passion was now even doing battle with his love. His first steps in society and in the service had been successful, but two years before he had made a serious mistake. Eager to show his independence and get ahead, he had refused a post that was offered to him, hoping that the refusal would make him more valuable; but as it turned out, he had been too bold, and was passed over. And having, whether he liked it or not, taken on the position of an independent man, he had carried it off with great tact and good sense, behaving as if he held nothing against anyone, considered himself slighted in no way, and cared for nothing but to be left alone since he was enjoying himself. In reality he had stopped enjoying himself as far back as the year before, when he had gone away to Moscow. He felt that this independent posture of a man who might have done anything but cared to do nothing was already beginning to pall, that many people were starting to think he wasn't actually capable of anything beyond being a straightforward, good-natured fellow. His affair with Madame Karenina, by causing such a sensation and drawing such general attention, had given him a fresh distinction that quieted the gnawing worm of ambition for a while — but a week ago that worm had been stirred up again with new force. The friend of his childhood, a man from the same set, the same coterie, his comrade in the Corps of Pages, Serpuhovskoy, who had left school with him and had been his rival in class, in gymnastics, in their pranks and their dreams of glory, had just returned from Central Asia, where he had gained two steps in rank and an order rarely given to generals so young.

As soon as he arrived in Petersburg, people started talking about him as a newly risen star of the first magnitude. A schoolmate of Vronsky's, the same age as he was, he was now a general, expecting a command that might shape the course of political events; while Vronsky, however independent, brilliant, and beloved by a charming woman, was simply a cavalry captain whose independence everyone was happy to indulge. "Of course I don't envy Serpuhovskoy and never could; but his advancement shows me that all one has to do is watch one's chance, and a man like me may have a career made very quickly. Three years ago he was in exactly the position I'm in. If I retire, I burn my ships. If I stay in the army, I lose nothing. She herself said she didn't want to change her position.
