And with her love I can't envy Serpuhovskoy." And slowly twirling his mustaches, he got up from the table and walked around the room. His eyes were shining particularly brightly, and he was in that confident, calm, and contented frame of mind which always came over him after he had thoroughly faced his situation. Everything was straight and clear, just as after his previous days of reckoning. He shaved, took a cold bath, dressed, and went out.

title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: "We've come to fetch you. Your _lessive_ went on quite a while today," said Petritsky. "So — is it over?"

"It's over," Vronsky answered, smiling only with his eyes and twirling the ends of his mustaches as carefully as if, after the perfect order he had just brought to his affairs, any too bold or sudden movement might upset it.
"You always look as though you'd just come out of the bath afterward," said Petritsky. "I've come from Gritsky's" (that was what they called the colonel); "they're expecting you."
Vronsky, without answering, looked at his comrade, his mind on something else.
"Yes — is that music coming from his place?" he said, listening to the familiar sounds of polkas and waltzes drifting over. "What's the party for?"
"Serpuhovskoy has come."
"Aha!" said Vronsky. "I didn't know."
The smile in his eyes glinted brighter than ever.

Having decided once and for all that he was happy in his love, that he was sacrificing his ambition to it — having, in any case, taken up that position — Vronsky was incapable either of envying Serpuhovskoy or of being hurt that he hadn't come to him first on returning to the regiment. Serpuhovskoy was a good friend, and he was delighted he had come.
"Oh, I'm very glad!"

The colonel, Demin, had taken a large country house. The whole party was on the wide lower balcony. In the courtyard the first things to catch Vronsky's eye were a band of singers in white linen coats, standing by a barrel of vodka, and the robust, good-humored figure of the colonel surrounded by officers. He had walked out as far as the first step of the balcony and was shouting at full volume across the band — which was playing Offenbach's quadrille — waving his arms and giving orders to a few soldiers standing off to one side. A group of soldiers, a quartermaster, and several subalterns came up to the balcony along with Vronsky. The colonel went back to the table, came out again onto the steps with a tumbler in his hand, and proposed the toast: "To the health of our former comrade, the gallant general, Prince Serpuhovskoy. Hurrah!"
Behind the colonel came Serpuhovskoy, stepping out onto the steps smiling, glass in hand.

"You only get younger, Bondarenko," he said to the rosy-cheeked, smart-looking quartermaster standing just in front of him — a man still youngish-looking, though he was doing his second term of service.

It had been three years since Vronsky had seen Serpuhovskoy. He looked more robust, had let his whiskers grow, but was still the same graceful figure, whose face and form were even more striking for their softness and nobility than for their beauty. The only change Vronsky noticed in him was that subdued, steady radiance of contentment that settles on the faces of men who are successful and sure that their success is acknowledged by everyone. Vronsky knew that radiant air, and spotted it in Serpuhovskoy at once.

Coming down the steps, Serpuhovskoy caught sight of Vronsky. A smile of pleasure lit up his face. He tossed his head back and waved the glass in his hand at Vronsky in greeting, showing him by the gesture that he couldn't come over before dealing with the quartermaster, who was standing with his lips already pushed forward to be kissed.
"Here he is!" the colonel shouted. "Yashvin told me you were in one of your gloomy moods."
Serpuhovskoy kissed the moist, fresh lips of the dashing-looking quartermaster, wiped his mouth with his handkerchief, and came over to Vronsky.
"How glad I am!" he said, squeezing his hand and pulling him aside.
"You look after him," the colonel shouted to Yashvin, pointing at Vronsky, and went down to the soldiers.
"Why weren't you at the races yesterday? I'd expected to see you there," said Vronsky, studying Serpuhovskoy.

"I did go, but late. Sorry about that," he added, and turned to the adjutant: "Please divide this up from me — however much it comes to per man." And he hurriedly took notes for three hundred roubles out of his pocketbook, blushing slightly.
"Vronsky! Want something to eat or drink?" Yashvin asked. "Hey, something for the count to eat! Ah, here it is — have a glass!"

The party at the colonel's went on for a long time. There was a great deal of drinking. They tossed Serpuhovskoy in the air and caught him again several times. Then they did the same to the colonel. Then, to the accompaniment of the band, the colonel himself danced with Petritsky. Then the colonel, who was starting to flag, sat down on a bench in the courtyard and began explaining to Yashvin the superiority of Russia over Prussia, especially in cavalry charges, and the revelry lulled for a moment. Serpuhovskoy went into the house to the bathroom to wash his hands and found Vronsky there; Vronsky was dousing his head with water. He had taken off his coat and stuck his sunburned, hairy neck under the tap, rubbing it and his head with his hands. When he was done, Vronsky sat down beside Serpuhovskoy. They both took seats on a lounge in the bathroom, and a conversation began that was very interesting to both of them.
"I've always heard about you through my wife," said Serpuhovskoy. "I'm glad you've been seeing her pretty often."

"She's friends with Varya, and they're the only women in Petersburg I care to see," Vronsky answered, smiling. He smiled because he could see what direction the conversation was about to take, and he was glad of it.
"The only ones?" Serpuhovskoy asked back, smiling.

"Yes — and I'd been hearing news of you, and not only through your wife," said Vronsky, cutting off the hint with a stern look. "I was delighted to hear of your success, though not at all surprised. I'd expected even more."
Serpuhovskoy smiled. Such an opinion of him was obviously pleasing, and he didn't see the point of hiding it.
"Well — I, on the contrary, had expected less; I'll admit that honestly. But I'm glad, very glad. I'm ambitious; that's my weakness, and I own up to it."
"Perhaps you wouldn't own up to it if you hadn't succeeded," said Vronsky.

"I don't suppose so," said Serpuhovskoy, smiling again. "I won't go as far as saying life wouldn't be worth living without it, but it would be dull. Of course I may be wrong, but I do think I have a certain talent for the line I've chosen, and that any power that comes into my hands, if it does, will be better there than in the hands of plenty of men I know," said Serpuhovskoy, with the radiant consciousness of success. "And so the closer I get to it, the better pleased I am."
"Maybe that's true for you, but not for everyone. I used to think the same way, but here I am, and I find life worth living for more than just that."

"There it is! Here it comes!" said Serpuhovskoy, laughing. "Ever since I heard about you, about your refusal, I began... Of course, I approved of what you did. But there are ways of doing everything. I think your action was good in itself, but you didn't go about it quite the way you should have."
"What's done is done, and you know I never go back on what I've done. Besides, I'm quite well off as I am."

"Quite well off — for now. But you're not satisfied with that. I wouldn't say this to your brother. He's a nice child, like our host here. Listen to him go!" he added, hearing the roar of "hurrah!" — "and he's happy, but that doesn't satisfy you."
"I didn't say it did."
"Yes, but that's not the only thing. Men like you are needed."
"By whom?"
"By whom? By society, by Russia. Russia needs men; she needs a party — otherwise everything goes, and will go, to the dogs."
"What do you mean? Bertenev's party against the Russian communists?"

"No," said Serpuhovskoy, frowning in annoyance at being suspected of anything so absurd. "_Tout ça est une blague_. That's always been around and always will be. There are no communists. But scheming people have to invent a noxious, dangerous party. It's an old trick. No — what's needed is a powerful party of independent men like you and me."
"But why?" Vronsky named several men currently in power. "Why aren't they independent men?"

"Simply because they don't have, or never had from birth, an independent fortune; they haven't had a name, they haven't been close to the sun and center the way we have. They can be bought either with money or with favor. And they have to find themselves a foothold by inventing some policy. So they come up with some notion, some program they don't really believe in, that does damage; and the whole policy is really just a means to a government house and so much income. _Cela n'est pas plus fin que ça_, once you get a glimpse of their cards. I may be inferior to them, perhaps stupider — though I don't see why I should be. But you and I do have one decisive advantage over them, in being harder to buy. And such men are needed now more than ever."

Vronsky listened attentively, but it wasn't so much the content of the words that interested him as Serpuhovskoy's attitude — already contemplating a struggle with the powers that be, already with his likes and dislikes set out in that higher world, while Vronsky's own interest in the governing sphere went no further than the interests of his regiment. Vronsky also felt how powerful Serpuhovskoy might become through his unmistakable gift for thinking things through and grasping situations, through his intelligence and his way with words, qualities he rarely encountered in the world he moved in. And, ashamed as he was of the feeling, he felt envious.
"Still, I lack the one thing that matters most for that," he answered; "I don't want power. I did once — but it's gone."
"Forgive me, but that isn't true," Serpuhovskoy said, smiling.
"Yes — it is true, it is true... now!" Vronsky added, to be honest.
"Yes, it's true now, that's a separate matter; but this _now_ won't last forever."
"Perhaps," Vronsky answered.

"You say _perhaps_," Serpuhovskoy went on, as if reading his thoughts, "but I say _for certain_. And that's why I wanted to see you. Your action was just what it should have been. I see that, but you shouldn't keep it up. All I'm asking is that you give me _carte blanche_. I'm not offering my protection... though, after all, why shouldn't I protect you? You've protected me often enough. I'd hope our friendship rises above that sort of thing. Yes," he said, smiling at him as tenderly as a woman, "give me _carte blanche_, retire from the regiment, and I'll draw you up by degrees."
"But you have to understand that I want nothing," said Vronsky, "except that everything should stay as it is."
Serpuhovskoy got up and stood facing him.

"You say everything should stay as it is. I understand what that means. But listen: we're the same age, and you've probably known more women than I have." Serpuhovskoy's smile and gestures told Vronsky he needn't be uneasy — that he would be gentle and careful in touching the sore spot. "But I'm married, and believe me, in getting to know thoroughly one's own wife, if one loves her, as someone has said, one comes to know all women better than if one had known thousands of them."
"We're coming, right away!" Vronsky shouted to an officer who looked into the room and called them to the colonel.
Vronsky was now longing to hear Serpuhovskoy out, to know what he was going to say to him.

"And here's my opinion for you. Women are the chief stumbling block in a man's career. It's hard to love a woman and do anything else. There's only one way to have love conveniently without its getting in the way — and that's marriage. How am I to put it?" said Serpuhovskoy, who loved analogies. "Wait a minute, wait a minute! Yes — just as you can only carry a _fardeau_ and still use your hands when the _fardeau_ is strapped to your back, and that's marriage. That's what I felt once I was married. My hands were suddenly set free. But to lug that _fardeau_ around without marriage, your hands will always be so full that you can't do anything else. Look at Mazankov, at Krupov. They've ruined their careers for the sake of women."
"What women, though!" said Vronsky, recalling the Frenchwoman and the actress the two men he'd named were involved with.
"The more firmly the woman is established in society, the worse it is. It's much the same as — not just carrying the _fardeau_ in your arms — but tearing it away from someone else."
"You've never loved," Vronsky said softly, looking straight ahead and thinking of Anna.
"Perhaps. But remember what I've said to you. And one more thing — women are all more materialistic than men. We make something enormous out of love, but they're always _terre-à-terre_."
"Right away, right away!" he called to a footman who came in. But the footman hadn't come to call them again, as he had assumed. The footman was bringing Vronsky a note.
"A man brought it from Princess Tverskaya."
Vronsky opened the letter and went crimson.
"My head's started to ache; I'm going home," he said to Serpuhovskoy.
"Oh, goodbye then. So — you give me _carte blanche?_"
"We'll talk about it later; I'll look you up in Petersburg."

title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: It was already six o'clock. To get there fast — and without taking his own horses, which everyone in town would recognize — Vronsky climbed into Yashvin's hired fly and told the driver to push the pace. It was a roomy, old-fashioned fly with seats for four. He sank into one corner, stretched his legs across to the front seat, and fell into thought.

A vague sense that his affairs had been put in order, a vague memory of Serpuhovskoy's friendliness and flattery — Serpuhovskoy, who had treated him as a man the country needed — and, above everything, the anticipation of the meeting ahead of him: all of it blended into a single, joyful feeling of being alive. The feeling was so strong he found himself smiling. He let his legs drop, crossed one knee over the other, took the calf in his hand, and felt the springy muscle where it had been grazed in his fall the day before. Then he leaned back and drew several deep breaths.

"I'm happy, very happy!" he said to himself. He had often felt this kind of physical joy in his own body before, but he had never been so fond of himself, of his own body, as he was now. He liked the slight ache in his strong leg; he liked the muscular sensation of his chest moving as he breathed. The bright, cold August day that had made Anna feel so hopeless struck him as keenly invigorating, refreshing his face and neck — which still tingled from the cold water he had splashed on himself. The scent of brilliantine on his whiskers seemed especially pleasant in the fresh air. Everything he saw through the carriage window — everything in that cold, pure air, in the pale light of the sunset — was as fresh and gay and strong as he was: the roofs of the houses gleaming in the sunset, the sharp edges of fences and the corners of buildings, the figures of passers-by, the carriages he met now and then, the still green of trees and grass, the fields with their evenly drawn potato furrows, and the slanting shadows that fell from the houses and trees and bushes — even from the rows of potatoes. The whole scene shone like a pretty landscape just painted and freshly varnished.

"On, on!" he called to the driver, leaning his head out of the window. He pulled a three-rouble note from his pocket and handed it over as the man looked back. The driver fumbled with something at the lamp, the whip cracked, and the carriage rolled swiftly along the smooth highroad.

"I want nothing — nothing but this happiness," he thought, staring at the bone bell-button in the space between the windows and picturing Anna exactly as he had seen her last. "And the longer this goes on, the more I love her. Here's the garden of the Vrede Villa. Where will she be? Where? How? Why did she choose this place to meet me, and why does she write to me through Betsy's letter?" — questions he was only now wondering about for the first time. But there was no time left for wondering. He called to the driver to stop before the avenue, opened the door, jumped out of the moving carriage, and walked up the avenue toward the house. The avenue was empty, but glancing to the right he caught sight of her. Her face was hidden by a veil, but his eyes drank in the way of walking that was hers and no one else's — the slope of the shoulders, the set of the head — and at once a kind of electric shock ran through him. He felt himself with renewed force, from the springy motion of his legs to the working of his lungs, and something made his lips twitch.
When she reached him, she pressed his hand tightly.
"You're not angry that I sent for you? I absolutely had to see you," she said. The serious, set line of her lips, visible under the veil, changed his mood at once.
"Angry — me! But how did you get here? Where did you come from?"
"Never mind," she said, laying her hand on his. "Come — I have to talk to you."

He understood that something had happened, and that this would not be a happy meeting. In her presence his will dissolved: without even knowing what was upsetting her, he felt the same distress passing into him unconsciously.
"What is it? What?" he asked, pressing her hand against his elbow and searching her face for her thoughts.
She walked on a few paces in silence, gathering her courage; then she suddenly stopped.

"I didn't tell you yesterday," she began, breathing quickly and painfully, "that when I came home with Alexey Alexandrovitch I told him everything... told him I couldn't be his wife, that... and told him everything."
He listened, his whole body unconsciously bending toward her as if to ease the weight of her position. But the moment she said it, he straightened up, and a proud, hard expression came over his face.

"Yes, yes — that's better, a thousand times better. I know how painful it was for you," he said. But she wasn't listening to his words. She was reading his thoughts from his face. She couldn't guess that the expression came from the first idea that had occurred to Vronsky — that a duel was now inevitable. A duel had never crossed her mind, and so she read his momentary hardness in a different way.

When she had received her husband's letter, she had known in the bottom of her heart that everything would go on as before — that she wouldn't have the strength of will to give up her position, abandon her son, and join her lover. The morning at Princess Tverskaya's had only confirmed it. Still, this meeting mattered to her enormously. She hoped it would transform her position and save her. If on hearing the news he said to her firmly, passionately, without an instant's hesitation, "Throw it all up and come with me!" — then she would give up her son and go away with him. But the news had not produced in him what she had hoped for; he simply looked as though he were nursing some affront.
"It wasn't in the least painful for me. It happened on its own," she said irritably. "And look...." She pulled her husband's letter out of her glove.

"I understand, I understand," he interrupted, taking the letter without reading it, trying to soothe her. "The one thing I longed for, the one thing I prayed for, was to put an end to this situation, so I could devote my life to your happiness."
"Why are you telling me that?" she said. "Do you think I can doubt it? If I doubted...."
"Who's that coming?" Vronsky said suddenly, pointing at two ladies walking toward them. "They may know us!" He turned aside hurriedly, pulling her with him into a side path.

"Oh, what does it matter!" she said. Her lips were trembling. And he imagined her eyes were looking at him with a strange fury from under the veil. "I tell you that's not the point — I can't doubt that. But look at what he writes me. Read it." She stopped again.

Just as in the first moment when he had heard of her rupture with her husband, Vronsky, on reading the letter, was carried away without realizing it by the natural reaction his relationship to the betrayed husband stirred in him. Holding the letter in his hands now, he couldn't help picturing the challenge he would probably find waiting for him at home today or tomorrow — and the duel itself, in which, with the same cold and haughty expression his face wore at this moment, he would stand ready for the injured husband's shot after firing into the air himself. And in that same instant, the thought flashed through his mind of what Serpuhovskoy had just said to him, of what he himself had been thinking that morning — that it was better not to tie himself down — and he knew this was a thought he could not share with her.

When he had finished reading, he raised his eyes to her, and there was no resolve in them. She saw at once that he had already been turning this over in his own mind. She knew that whatever he might say to her, he wouldn't say everything he was thinking. And she knew her last hope had failed. This was not what she had been counting on.
"You see the sort of man he is," she said, her voice shaking. "He...."

"Forgive me, but I'm glad of it," Vronsky interrupted. "For God's sake, let me finish!" he added, his eyes begging her to give him time to explain. "I'm glad, because things can't — they simply can't — stay the way he supposes they will."
"Why can't they?" Anna said, holding back her tears, clearly attaching no weight to anything he said. She felt her fate was sealed.
Vronsky meant that after the duel — which he considered unavoidable — things couldn't continue as before, but what came out was something else.
"It can't go on. I hope that now you'll leave him. I hope" — he was flustered, and reddened — "that you'll let me arrange our life and plan it. Tomorrow...." he was beginning.
She did not let him go on.
"But my child!" she cried. "Look what he writes! I'd have to leave him, and I can't and won't do that."
"But for God's sake — which is better? Leave your child, or keep up this degrading position?"
"To whom is it degrading?"
"To everyone, and most of all to you."

"You say degrading.... Don't say that. Those words have no meaning for me," she said with a trembling voice. She did not want him now to say anything untrue. All she had left was his love, and she wanted to love him. "Don't you see that from the day I loved you everything has changed for me? For me there is one thing, and one thing only — your love. If that is mine, I feel so lifted up, so strong, that nothing can humiliate me. I am proud of my position, because... proud of being... proud...." She couldn't say what she was proud of. Tears of shame and despair choked her voice. She stopped and sobbed.

He too felt something swelling in his throat and twitching at his nose, and for the first time in his life he felt on the verge of tears. He couldn't have said exactly what touched him so. He was sorry for her, and he felt he could not help her, and along with that he knew he was the cause of her misery, and that he had done something wrong.
"Is a divorce out of the question?" he asked weakly. She shook her head without answering. "Couldn't you take your son and still leave him?"
"Yes — but it all depends on him. I have to go to him now," she said shortly. Her presentiment that everything would simply continue as before had not deceived her.
"I'll be in Petersburg on Tuesday, and everything can be settled."
"Yes," she said. "But let's not talk about it anymore."
Anna's carriage, which she had sent away and ordered to come back to the small gate of the Vrede garden, drove up. Anna said goodbye to Vronsky and drove home.

title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: On Monday the Commission of the 2nd of June held its usual sitting. Alexey Alexandrovitch walked into the hall, greeted the members and the president as he always did, and took his seat, laying his hand on the papers already arranged in front of him. Among them were the necessary documents and a rough draft of the speech he meant to deliver. But he did not really need any of it. He remembered every point and saw no reason to rehearse mentally what he would say. He knew that when the moment came, and when he saw his enemy across from him studiously trying to look indifferent, the speech would flow of itself better than he could prepare it now. He felt that what he was about to say carried such weight that every word would tell. While the routine report was read, he kept the most harmless, inoffensive air. No one watching his white hands, with their swollen veins and long fingers gently stroking the edges of the white paper, or the air of weariness with which his head tilted to one side, would have suspected that in a few minutes a torrent of words would burst from his lips — a flood that would raise a storm, set the members shouting and attacking one another, and force the president to call for order. When the report ended, Alexey Alexandrovitch announced in his quiet, refined voice that he had several points to bring before the meeting concerning the Commission for the Reorganization of the Native Tribes. Every eye turned to him. He cleared his throat, and, instead of looking at his opponent, fixed his eyes — as he always did while speaking — on the first person sitting opposite him, an inoffensive little old man who had never had a single opinion in the Commission, and began to lay out his views. When he reached the point about the fundamental and radical law, his opponent jumped up and started to protest. Stremov, also a member of the Commission and stung to the quick, began defending himself, and the sitting turned stormy; but Alexey Alexandrovitch triumphed. His motion was carried, three new commissions were appointed, and the next day a certain Petersburg circle talked of nothing but the sitting. Alexey Alexandrovitch's success had been even greater than he had expected.

The next morning, Tuesday, Alexey Alexandrovitch woke remembering with pleasure his triumph of the previous day, and he couldn't help smiling — though he tried to look indifferent — when the chief secretary of his department, eager to flatter him, passed on the rumors that had reached him about what had happened in the Commission.

Absorbed in business with the chief secretary, Alexey Alexandrovitch had completely forgotten that it was Tuesday, the day he had fixed for Anna Arkadyevna's return, and he was startled and irritated when a servant came in to tell him she had arrived.

Anna had reached Petersburg early that morning; the carriage had been sent to meet her in accordance with her telegram, so Alexey Alexandrovitch could have known of her arrival. But when she came in, he did not go out to meet her. She was told he hadn't yet gone out, but was busy with his secretary. She sent word that she had come, went to her own room, and busied herself sorting her things, expecting him to come to her. But an hour went by, and he did not come. She went into the dining-room on the pretext of giving some orders, and spoke loudly on purpose, hoping he would come out to her; but he did not, though she heard him go to the door of his study as he saw the chief secretary off. She knew he usually left quickly for his office, and she wanted to see him before he did, so that the terms between them could be made clear.

She walked across the drawing-room and went straight to him. When she entered his study he was in his official uniform, plainly ready to go out, sitting at a small table with his elbows on it, staring dejectedly in front of him. She saw him before he saw her, and she could tell he was thinking of her.

When he saw her, he was about to rise, then changed his mind; then his face flushed a deep red — something Anna had never seen before. He got up quickly and went to meet her, not looking at her eyes but at a point above them, at her forehead and hair. He came up to her, took her hand, and asked her to sit down.

"I'm very glad you've come," he said, sitting down beside her, and clearly wanting to say something he stammered. Several times he tried to begin and stopped. Although she had prepared herself to despise and reproach him during the meeting, she didn't know what to say, and she felt sorry for him. So the silence stretched on. "Is Seryozha quite well?" he said, and without waiting for an answer added: "I shan't be dining at home today, and I have to go out directly."
"I had thought of going to Moscow," she said.
"No, you were quite, quite right to come," he said, and fell silent again.
Seeing he was incapable of starting the conversation, she began it herself.

"Alexey Alexandrovitch," she said, looking at him and not dropping her eyes under his steady stare at her hair, "I'm a guilty woman, I'm a bad woman, but I am the same as I was, as I told you then, and I have come to tell you that I can change nothing."

"I have asked you no question about that," he said, suddenly, decisively, looking her straight in the face with hatred. "That was what I had supposed." Anger seemed to give him back full command of all his faculties. "But as I told you then, and have written to you," he went on in a thin, shrill voice, "I repeat now: I am not obliged to know this. I ignore it. Not all wives are as kind as you, so quick to bring such pleasant news to their husbands." He emphasized the word "pleasant." "I shall continue to ignore it as long as the world knows nothing of it, as long as my name is not disgraced. So I simply inform you that our relations must be just as they have always been, and that only in the event of your compromising me will I be obliged to take steps to protect my honor."
"But our relations cannot be the same as always," Anna began in a timid voice, looking at him in dismay.

Once again seeing his composed gestures and hearing that shrill, childish, sarcastic voice, her revulsion for him snuffed out her pity, and she felt only afraid — but at all costs she meant to make her position clear.
"I cannot be your wife while I...." she began.
He laughed a cold, malignant laugh.

"I suppose the manner of life you have chosen is reflected in your ideas. I have too much respect — or contempt — or both... I respect your past and despise your present... so that the interpretation you put on my words was far from what I meant."
Anna sighed and bowed her head.

"Though I really fail to see how, with the independence you display" — he was warming to it now — "announcing your infidelity to your husband and apparently seeing nothing improper in it, you can find anything improper in fulfilling a wife's duties toward her husband."
"Alexey Alexandrovitch! What is it you want of me?"

"I want you not to meet that man here, and to conduct yourself so that neither the world nor the servants can reproach you... that you not see him. That isn't much, I think. And in return you will have all the privileges of a faithful wife without fulfilling her duties. That's all I have to say to you. Now I must go. I'm not dining at home." He got up and moved toward the door.
Anna got up too. He bowed in silence and let her pass before him.
